title: Fundamentals of gravitational radiation
one_line_summary: Takes the linearized field equations of Chapter 8 into the time-dependent regime: shows that vacuum perturbations are light-speed waves with exactly two transverse-traceless polarizations, explains how they tidally distort free masses and how bars, radar ranging and laser interferometers sense that distortion, derives the slow-motion quadrupole formula for their generation, obtains their energy flux from a Feynman sticky-bead style energy-balance argument, applies the results to the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar, and ends with chirp-mass scaling and the idea of binaries as standard sirens.
role_in_book: This is the first of the book's astrophysical chapters in the third edition's reorganized arc. It sits directly after the weak-field chapter because gravitational waves are the simplest departure from special relativity predicted by Einstein's equations: they need only the linearized equations, Lorenz gauge and geodesic deviation already built in Chapters 6-8. The chapter supplies the vocabulary (TT gauge, strain h, polarization, quadrupole luminosity, chirp mass, standard siren) that Chapters 10-11 use when discussing neutron stars and black holes as sources, that Chapter 12 uses to interpret the LIGO-Virgo detections, and that Chapter 13 uses when gravitational-wave distances and the primordial background enter cosmology. It opens with a short framing section recasting general relativity as central to modern astronomy rather than a theory of tiny corrections.

Equation of geodesic deviation and the connecting vector
Local inertial frames where Christoffel symbols vanish at a point
One-forms, null vectors, raising and lowering with eta
Stress-energy tensor, its conservation, and T^00 approximately equal to rest-mass density for slow sources
Geometrized units G = c = 1, masses and times in meters
Forced damped harmonic oscillator, resonance, quality factor
Kepler circular orbits and Newtonian binding energy of a binary
Wave equation, plane waves, complex exponential notation, Fourier superposition

Equipartition: thermal energy k_B T per oscillator mode
Pulsars, parsecs, standard candles, cosmological redshift

learning_objectives: Reader can show that a plane-wave ansatz solves the vacuum linearized equations only if the wave one-form is null, and conclude that gravitational waves travel at light speed without dispersion.
Reader can use the Lorenz gauge condition and the residual gauge freedom to reduce the wave amplitude to transverse-traceless form, and count the two remaining physical degrees of freedom.
Reader can explain why free particles stay at fixed TT coordinates yet their proper separation oscillates, and compute the fractional change in separation as one half of h_xx^TT.

Reader can write the geodesic-deviation equation in a local inertial frame for a wave, express the relevant Riemann components through second time derivatives of h^TT, and add non-gravitational forces to treat bound systems such as rulers and bars.
Reader can draw the deformation of a ring of test particles for plus and cross polarizations and explain why these are rotated by 45 degrees rather than 90 degrees.
Reader can derive the forced damped oscillator equation for an idealized bar detector, find its resonant amplitude and energy, and estimate numbers for a Weber bar and the thermal-noise requirement.

Reader can compute light round-trip times in a gravitational-wave metric to first order, derive the rate of change of return time, and explain why an interferometer does not care whether the light's wavelength is stretched.

Reader can describe the main noise sources (seismic, thermal, shot) and the frequency bands of ground interferometers, LISA, pulsar timing and CMB polarization, and explain why networks are needed for sky position and polarization.

Reader can derive the slow-motion quadrupole field of a periodic source from the wave equation using Gauss's theorem, and explain why energy-momentum conservation removes monopole and dipole wave fields.

Reader can compute quadrupole moments and TT waveforms for a vibrating spring and an equal-mass circular binary, including the polarization seen along and perpendicular to the orbital axis and at general inclination.
Reader can make order-of-magnitude estimates of wave amplitude (h of order M/r times v^2) and explain why a wave can be detectable when the static Newtonian field of the same source is not.

Reader can reconstruct the energy-balance argument that fixes the gravitational-wave energy flux F = Omega^2 A^2 / (32 pi), and integrate it over a sphere to obtain the quadrupole luminosity formula L = (1/5) <dddot I_ij dddot I^ij>.
Reader can estimate the period decay of the Hulse-Taylor binary from the circular-orbit formula and explain why eccentricity raises it by a factor of about 12.

Reader can define the chirp mass, show that luminosity, energy, chirp time, time to merger and remaining phase all depend on the dimensionless product of chirp mass and orbital frequency, and use this to explain why a binary is a standard siren whose distance follows from amplitude, frequency and frequency drift.
Reader can explain how cosmological redshift enters observed chirp masses and converts the inferred distance into a luminosity distance.

teaching_approach.summary: A long chapter that mixes compact tensor derivations with extended, up-to-date instrumentation and astrophysics. Schutz repeatedly derives the same physical fact in two gauges or two ways (coordinate positions versus proper distance; metric integration versus geodesic deviation; energy absorbed by detectors versus amplitude reduction downstream) so that the reader learns to trust only invariant, measurable statements. Detectors are used as a pedagogical device, not just as hardware: the bar oscillator is first a detector, then a radiator, then the device that fixes the energy flux before dropping out. The final section leans on dimensional analysis and scale-freedom to turn the quadrupole formula into observational tools (chirp mass, standard sirens).
narrative_arc: Frame: general relativity is not just tiny corrections; gravitational waves, neutron stars and black holes are now observed, and waves are the simplest non-Newtonian prediction.
Solve the vacuum linearized wave equation with a plane wave; nullity of k gives light-speed propagation and no dispersion.
Spend the residual gauge freedom to reach TT gauge; only two amplitudes survive.
Paradox: a free particle stays at fixed TT coordinates. Resolve by computing the proper distance between two particles, which does oscillate.
Re-derive the effect gauge-invariantly with geodesic deviation in a local inertial frame; reinterpret as a tidal force that can be added to other forces, answering why rulers do not stretch.
Picture the two polarizations with a ring of particles; exhibit an exact nonlinear plane wave and state how short waves propagate through curved spacetime.
Survey detection: frequency bands and detector families; analyze an idealized bar as a forced damped oscillator with realistic Weber-bar numbers and noise limits.

Compute radar round-trip times in the wave metric, derive the return-time derivative and the three-term relation, and build the interferometer as two perpendicular beam detectors; discuss LIGO optics, noise, networks, future ground detectors and LISA.
Close detection with the cosmic-sound analogy: coherent, phase-sensitive, nearly omnidirectional reception.
Generation: crude amplitude bound M/R, then slow-motion solution of the sourced wave equation via Gauss's theorem, conservation laws, tensor virial identity, quadrupole field and TT projection.

Apply to a vibrating spring (hopeless laboratory source) and to a circular binary (circular versus linear polarization, inclination dependence, Hulse-Taylor amplitude); make order-of-magnitude arguments and note spherical motions do not radiate; state the retarded-integral generalization.

Energy: Feynman sticky-bead motivation, sheet of oscillators absorbs energy and re-radiates a wave that interferes destructively downstream; equate to get F; generalize and integrate to the quadrupole luminosity; upper luminosity c^5/G.
Check against nature: period decay of the Hulse-Taylor pulsar, including the eccentricity correction and 0.17 percent agreement.

Standard sirens: unequal masses, chirp mass as the only scale, scaling laws for chirp time, merger time, remaining phase and luminosity; distance from amplitude; redshifted masses and luminosity distance; eccentricity decay.
signature_moves: Pose an apparent paradox created by a coordinate choice (particles at rest in TT gauge; coordinate light speed not equal to 1) and dissolve it by computing an invariant.
Derive a result twice by independent routes and point out that the agreement is a consistency check (Eq. 9.24 versus 9.28; Eq. 9.45 via proper length versus geodesic deviation).
Recycle one toy system through the whole chapter: the two-mass spring is detector (§9.3), emitter (§9.4) and energy-flux calibrator (§9.5).
Insist that each metric component be treated as a scalar function when solving the wave equation, bringing tensor structure back only when conservation laws are applied.
Use geometrized units throughout and convert back only at the end, advertising that luminosity is dimensionless and c^5/G is the natural unit.
Quote realistic engineering and observational numbers (Weber bar mass and Q, 4-km arms, Q of 2 x 10^9 for suspensions, 2.5 million km LISA arms, measured period derivative) to calibrate intuition.
Extract physics from dimensional analysis and scale-freedom (h ~ phi_0 phi_r; L depends only on the remaining number of orbits).
Use sound as the governing analogy for gravitational-wave astronomy (listening, chirps, sirens, microphones).

sections.title: The role of general relativity in the physical Universe
sections.summary: A framing essay. Einstein saw the theory mainly as a fix for the conflict between special relativity and Newtonian gravity, doubted that black holes were physical and that gravitational waves were real or detectable. Schutz contrasts this with the modern situation: black holes and neutron stars are common, waves have been detected, and two Nobel prizes (binary pulsar 1993, LIGO 2017) have gone to gravitational-wave science. The section lays out the plan for Chapters 9-13.
key_moves: Replace the picture of GR as tiny corrections with GR as an observational science.
Name Einstein's worry that waves might be coordinate artifacts, a worry the chapter will answer with invariant measurements.
Motivate waves as the simplest non-Newtonian consequence of the field equations.

sections.title: The propagation of gravitational waves
sections.summary: Solves the vacuum linearized equations with a complex plane wave, finds the wave vector must be null (light-speed propagation, no dispersion) and the amplitude orthogonal to it (Lorenz gauge). A second gauge transformation generated by a plane-wave vector field imposes tracelessness and orthogonality to a chosen four-velocity, the TT gauge, leaving only A_xx = -A_yy and A_xy for a wave along z. Free particles stay at fixed TT coordinates, but the proper distance between neighbours oscillates by a fraction h_xx^TT/2. The same effect is recovered from geodesic deviation in a local inertial frame, where the Riemann components are minus one half of second time derivatives of h^TT; this turns the wave into a tidal force that can be combined with other forces, explaining why rigid rulers barely respond. The two polarizations are drawn as elliptical deformations of a particle ring rotated 45 degrees apart.
concepts: geodesic deviation in a gravitational wave
tidal force of a gravitational wave
stretching of space and rigid rulers
key_moves: Substitute exp(i k.x) into the wave equation: eta^{mu nu} k_mu k_nu = 0.
Gauge condition becomes A^{alpha beta} k_beta = 0.
Choose xi_alpha = B_alpha exp(i k.x) to set trace and A_{alpha beta} U^beta to zero; count remaining freedom.
In the rest frame of U with k along z, only xx, yy = -xx, xy survive.
Initial acceleration -Gamma^alpha_00 vanishes in TT gauge, so coordinate positions never change.
Proper distance along x is (1 + h_xx^TT/2) epsilon: invariant effect proportional to separation.
Geodesic deviation in local inertial frame: d^2 xi^j/dt^2 = -R^j_{0k0} xi^k with R_{x0x0} = -h_xx,00^TT/2.
Add F/m terms to the deviation equation to treat non-free bodies.

sections.title: Exact plane wave and waves in curved spacetime (end of §9.2)
sections.summary: Using null coordinates u = t - z and v = t + z, the metric -du dv + f(u)^2 dx^2 + g(u)^2 dy^2 is an exact vacuum solution provided f''/f + g''/g = 0; for g close to 1 it reduces to the linear plus-polarized wave, and free particles still stay at fixed coordinates. The subsection on geometrical optics states without derivation that short-wavelength waves on a curved background follow null geodesics and parallel-transport their polarization, like light, can be lensed, but are almost unaffected by matter, making them uniquely penetrating messengers.
key_moves: Guess a metric depending only on u that stretches only transverse directions.
Compute Christoffel symbols and R^x_{uxu} = -f''/f; vacuum equation is a single ODE.
Free function g(u) mirrors the arbitrary waveform of the linear theory.
State the two short-wavelength conditions (short compared with curvature radius and with background timescale).

sections.title: The detection of gravitational waves
sections.summary: Argues that the gravitational-wave spectrum is a new window, lists detector families and their bands (ground bars and interferometers above about 1 Hz, LISA in the millihertz band, spacecraft tracking, pulsar timing at nanohertz, CMB polarization at 1e-16 Hz). Models a bar detector as two masses on a damped spring in TT coordinates, deriving a forced damped oscillator driven by l_0 h_xx,00^TT/2, then finds the steady resonant amplitude and energy and plugs in Weber-bar numbers (amplitude of order 1e-15 m, energy of order 1e-20 J). Discusses thermal noise and cryogenics, pendulum isolation, transducers and the quantum limit. Then computes photon round-trip times in the wave metric, obtains the return-time derivative and the three-term formula, and explains interferometers as two beam detectors in which one arm acts as the clock for the other. Describes Fabry-Perot arm cavities, power recycling, suspension Q, shot noise, the 20 Hz-2 kHz band, networks for localization and polarization, third-generation plans, LISA's time-delay interferometry and drag-free proof masses, and closes with the cosmic-sound analogy.
concepts: return-time response of a beam detector
Fabry-Perot arm cavities and power recycling
key_moves: Newton's law holds in a local inertial frame that coincides with TT coordinates to first order for slow motions.
Spring force depends on proper length l = (x2 - x1)(1 + h_xx^TT/2).
Eliminate coordinate separation to get xi'' + 2 gamma xi' + omega_0^2 xi = l_0 h_xx,00^TT / 2.
Resonance: R = l_0 A Q/2 and E = m l_0^2 Omega^2 A^2 Q^2 / 16.
Photon coordinate speed (1 + h_+)^{-1/2} along x; integrate with unperturbed path inside h_+.
Differentiate return time with respect to emission time: only h at emission and at return matter (for normal incidence).
Interferometer compares two return times, so laser wavelength changes are irrelevant.
Plus wave overhead stretches one arm and squeezes the other; cross wave overhead gives no signal.

sections.title: Interferometers, networks, future detectors and cosmic sound (§9.3 continued)
sections.summary: Spacecraft tracking as the simplest beam detector and its limits (plasma, clock stability near 1e-19 would miss amplitudes of 1e-20); the interferometer as clock-free comparison of two arms; LIGO's first detection on 14 September 2015 and the binary neutron star of 17 August 2017; noise budget and data analysis ('LIGO is a 1e-22 detector'); networks of three or more detectors for triangulation and two for polarization when position is known; LIGO-India, KAGRA, Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, LISA (three spacecraft, 2.5e6 km arms, 60-degree opening angle, transponded beams, TDI, drag-free operation proven by LISA Pathfinder), DECIGO for the decihertz gap; analogy with acoustics.
key_moves: Three-term formula lets a true wave be distinguished from local plasma noise because it appears three times with a sign flip.
Arrival-time delays between two sites define a ring on the sky; a third detector cuts it to two patches.
Inclination follows from the degree of circular polarization.
Gravity has one sign of charge, so bulk mass motions add coherently, as pressure changes do for sound.

sections.title: The generation of gravitational waves
sections.summary: Starts with the bound h of order M/R for a source of mass M at distance R, applied to a supernova black hole and to GW150914 (implying 10 percent-level metric distortion near the merger). Solves the sourced wave equation for a sinusoidal, compact, slow-moving source: outside the source the outgoing solution is A e^{i Omega r}/r; integrating over a small ball with Gauss's theorem gives A = 4 J with J the integrated source. Conservation of T^{mu nu} forces the time-dependent J^{mu 0} to vanish, and the tensor virial identity turns J_ij into second time derivatives of the mass quadrupole, giving the quadrupole approximation. Projection to TT gauge along z gives the waveform in terms of the reduced quadrupole. Examples: vibrating spring (radiates at omega and 2 omega, no radiation along its axis, laboratory amplitude negligibly small) and equal-mass circular binary (frequency 2 omega, circular polarization along the axis, linear in the plane, general inclination formula, Hulse-Taylor numbers). Order-of-magnitude reasoning gives h ~ phi_0 phi_r and explains why wave tidal forces beat static Newtonian tides by (phi_0 r/R)^2; spherically symmetric motion does not radiate; a rotating square shows the danger of trusting the leading-order formula. Closes with the retarded-integral generalization to arbitrary time dependence.
concepts: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation
no gravitational radiation from spherically symmetric motion
key_moves: Treat each component of h-bar as an independent scalar solving the wave equation.
Integrate (nabla^2 + Omega^2) B = -16 pi S over a ball of radius epsilon << wavelength; the Omega^2 term is negligible and the Laplacian becomes a surface flux -4 pi A.
Use T^{mu nu},nu = 0 and Gauss's theorem to show J^{mu 0} = 0 for Omega not zero.
Use d^2/dt^2 of integral T^00 x^l x^m = 2 integral T^lm to write h-bar_jk = -2 Omega^2 D_jk e^{...}/r.
TT-project along the propagation direction: h_xx^TT = -Omega^2 (I_xx - I_yy) e/r, h_xy^TT = -2 Omega^2 I_xy e/r.
For the binary, the i in I_xy produces a quarter-period lag: circular polarization along the axis.
Virial theorem v^2 ~ phi_0 converts M v^2/r into phi_0 phi_r.

sections.title: The energy carried away by gravitational waves
sections.summary: Recalls the historical confusion over whether waves carry energy and Feynman's sticky-bead resolution. A plane of damped oscillators at areal density sigma absorbs power m gamma <xi'^2> per oscillator from an incident plus wave. Each oscillator also radiates via the quadrupole formula; summing over the plane with a convergence factor gives a net plane wave that, after TT projection, reduces the downstream amplitude by 2 pi sigma m Omega l_0 R sin phi. Dividing the power lost by the amplitude change eliminates all oscillator parameters, yielding dF/dA = Omega^2 A/(16 pi) and hence F = Omega^2 A^2/(32 pi) = Omega^2 <h_mu nu^TT h^TT mu nu>/(32 pi). Schutz stresses that this assumes energy conservation and is valid only in linearized theory. Evaluating F on a sphere with the angular integrals of n^i n^j and n^i n^j n^k n^l gives L = (1/5) Omega^6 <I_ij I^ij>, or L = (1/5) <dddot I_ij dddot I^ij> in general; order-of-magnitude scaling L ~ phi_0^5 and an absolute bound L of order c^5/G.
concepts: energy flux of a gravitational wave
key_moves: Energy absorbed per oscillator: <dE/dt> = m gamma Omega^2 R^2 / 2.
Field of one oscillator from Eq. 9.93 with A -> R/2; integrate over the plane using varpi d varpi = r dr and a damping factor exp(-epsilon r).
Superposing with the incident wave leaves a slightly phase-shifted downstream wave whose amplitude is lower by 2 pi sigma m Omega l_0 R times sin phi.
Divide delta F by delta A, eliminate R and phi with Eqs. 9.48-9.49: oscillator properties cancel.
Write the flux covariantly under background Lorentz transformations and apply to any small patch of wavefront.
Replace the special z direction by n^j and integrate over angles using symmetric-tensor identities.
Radiation energy within radius R gives Newtonian potential of order L, which cannot exceed about 1 without forming a black hole.

sections.title: An example: the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar (end of §9.5)
sections.summary: Applies the luminosity formula to an equal-mass circular binary: L = (8/5) M^2 l_0^4 omega^6 = 4.0 (M omega)^{10/3}. With PSR B1913+16 numbers (P = 27907 s, M = 1.4 solar masses = 2.07 km) the circular-orbit luminosity is 1.71e-29 in geometrized units and the orbital energy -1.11e-3 m. Logarithmic differentiation of E(omega) gives dP/dt of about -2.0e-13; the eccentricity e = 0.617 raises the loss rate about twelvefold. The GR prediction -2.40263e-12 agrees with the observed -(2.398 +/- 0.004)e-12 to 0.17 percent.
key_moves: Write the Newtonian binding energy of the circular orbit first with the orbital radius, then eliminate the radius with Kepler's law so it scales as the 5/3 power of mass times the 2/3 power of orbital frequency.
d ln E = (2/3) d ln omega = -(2/3) d ln P, and dE/dt = -L.
dP/dt = 3PL/(2E) is dimensionless in any unit system.
Explain the factor 12 by the steep omega^6 dependence at periastron.

sections.title: Standard sirens
sections.summary: Generalizes binary radiation to unequal masses and finds that amplitudes depend on the masses only through mu M^{2/3}, which defines the chirp mass. Written with the chirp mass, waveform, luminosity (32/5)(M omega)^{10/3} and energy -(1/2) M (M omega)^{2/3} show that the chirp mass is the only scale, a manifestation of the scale-free character of gravity. Energy balance gives the chirp mass from omega and its time derivative, and scaling laws for chirp time, time to merger (3/8 of the chirp time), remaining orbital phase, and a mass-independent luminosity L = 1/(160 psi^2). Because amplitude, frequency and frequency drift are measured, the distance follows: binaries are standard sirens, with inclination supplied by polarization measurements across a network. Redshift multiplies observed masses by (1+z) and makes the distance a luminosity distance, opening a route to the Hubble-Lemaitre constant. Eccentricity is radiated away faster than the orbit shrinks, so ground-based sources are nearly circular.
concepts: remaining orbital phase and mass-independent luminosity
key_moves: Replace m by 2 mu and eliminate l_0 with Kepler's law to get amplitudes proportional to mu M^{2/3} omega^{2/3}.
Double chirp mass, halve frequency, double distance and time: identical signal.
Solve dE/dt = -L for omega-dot: omega-dot = (96/5) M^{-2} (M omega)^{11/3}.
Integrate dt/d omega and d psi/d omega to infinity for merger time and phase.
Combine L(M omega) with psi(M omega) to eliminate the mass.
Distance r = alpha M (M omega)^{2/3}/h with alpha an O(1) orientation factor.
Frequencies and their derivatives redshift, so the inferred chirp mass is (1+z) times the source-frame value.

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: Annotated reading: Weber's bars and the controversy over his claimed detections (Collins), the history of doubts about wave reality (Kennefick, Blum et al.), quantum nondemolition and squeezed light, Living Reviews articles on post-Newtonian theory and interferometers, textbooks by Saulson, Creighton and Anderson, Maggiore, Andersson, Reitze-Saulson-Grote, and websites for detectors. It also credits Feynman's Chapel Hill 1957 sticky-bead argument (proceedings freely available) as the basis of §9.5, mentions Bondi, Pirani and Weber at that meeting, and notes that proving the quadrupole formula for strongly self-gravitating systems took decades.
key_moves: Point readers to variational and field-theoretic derivations of the flux that the book skips.
Flag that the linear-theory quadrupole formula's validity for relativistic binaries was established only later (Damour, Futamase, Blanchet).

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Fifty-six exercises that fill in derivations (TT gauge construction, Riemann components, oscillator response, quadrupole solution via multipole expansion and Bessel functions, angular integrals, luminosity), probe interpretation (does a freely falling bowl of soup slosh; radar distance measurement; gauge-equivalent metrics with identical curvature), and extend to astrophysics (unequal-mass and eccentric binaries, chirp-mass scaling laws, luminosity of merging black holes versus the Universe, Peters formulae for orbital decay).
concepts: energy flux of a gravitational wave
key_moves: Many exercises are explicitly the missing steps of the text, so they double as a guided reading.

concepts.name: gravitational waves
concepts.definition: Propagating, time-dependent perturbations of spacetime curvature that travel at the speed of light, are sourced by accelerating non-spherical mass-energy distributions, and carry energy and angular momentum away from their sources. In linearized theory they are wavelike vacuum solutions for the metric perturbation.
concepts.how_introduced: Framed historically (Einstein's 1916 prediction and later doubts) and then obtained as the non-static solutions of the vacuum weak-field equations that Chapter 8 had set aside when taking the Newtonian limit.

concepts.name: plane gravitational wave
concepts.definition: The complex solution h-bar^{alpha beta} = A^{alpha beta} exp(i k_mu x^mu) of the vacuum linearized equations with constant amplitude tensor and constant real wave one-form; the physical field is its real part, and by Fourier analysis every vacuum solution in Lorenz gauge is a superposition of such waves.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as an ansatz for the three-dimensional wave equation; substituting shows what k must satisfy, and the gauge condition then constrains A.
concepts.notes: Footnote 1 explains the complex-exponential convention; see also Exercise 9.3 on Fourier superposition.

concepts.name: null wave vector
concepts.definition: The wave one-form k_alpha of a plane wave, whose associated vector obeys eta^{mu nu} k_mu k_nu = 0; its time component is the angular frequency omega and its spatial part the wave vector. Nullity means a photon moving along k stays at constant wave phase, so the wave propagates at light speed in the direction of k.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from requiring the plane-wave ansatz to satisfy the wave equation, then interpreted by following a photon on x^mu = k^mu lambda + l^mu and noting its phase k_mu x^mu is constant.

concepts.name: dispersion relation
concepts.definition: The relation omega^2 = |k|^2 between frequency and wavenumber for gravitational waves in linearized vacuum theory, implying phase and group velocities both equal to 1 and no dispersion.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the nullity of k; Schutz notes that readers with wave-theory experience will recognize light-speed, dispersion-free propagation.

concepts.name: Lorenz gauge
concepts.definition: The coordinate condition that the divergence of the trace-reversed perturbation vanishes, h-bar^{alpha beta}_{,beta} = 0; it turns the linearized field equations into flat-space wave equations and, for a plane wave, forces the amplitude to be orthogonal to the wave vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 8 as the condition under which Eq. 9.1 holds; its consequence A^{alpha beta} k_beta = 0 is derived immediately.
concepts.notes: The book writes 'Lorentz gauge'; the historically correct attribution is to L. Lorenz.

concepts.name: residual gauge freedom
aliases: gauge freedom within the Lorenz class
concepts.definition: Infinitesimal coordinate changes generated by a vector field xi with box xi = 0 keep a perturbation in Lorenz gauge; for plane waves choosing xi_alpha = B_alpha exp(i k.x) shifts A by terms built from B and k, and the four constants B_alpha can be used to impose further conditions.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by recalling Eq. 8.38 and choosing a gauge vector with the same null k as the wave, then dividing out the common exponential to get an algebraic change of amplitude.
formulas: A^{(\rm NEW)}_{\alpha\beta}=A^{(\rm OLD)}_{\alpha\beta}-iB_\alpha k_\beta-iB_\beta k_\alpha+i\eta_{\alpha\beta}B^\mu k_\mu
concepts.notes: Exercise 9.5 shows only three of the four conditions A_{alpha beta}U^beta = 0 are independent, so trace plus these use up all four B's, and that TT gauge cannot be reached for static (omega = 0) fields.

concepts.name: transverse-traceless gauge
concepts.definition: The gauge in which, besides the Lorenz condition, the wave amplitude is traceless and orthogonal to a chosen constant four-velocity U. In the rest frame of U with propagation along z the surviving entries are A_xx, its negative in the yy slot, and the symmetric off-diagonal pair A_xy; the trace-reversed and ordinary perturbations coincide, and no gauge freedom remains, so the two surviving components are physical.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by spending the residual freedom on trace and U-orthogonality, then going to U's rest frame and aligning z with the wave; 'transverse' is explained by the vanishing of all components along the propagation direction.

concepts.name: plus and cross polarization
aliases: linear polarization states of gravitational waves
concepts.definition: The two independent linear polarization states of a gravitational wave: h_+ = h_xx^TT = -h_yy^TT stretches and squeezes a ring of free particles along the x and y axes, while h_x = h_xy^TT does the same along the diagonals. The two patterns are rotated by 45 degrees relative to each other, as expected for a symmetric rank-2 field, in contrast with the 90-degree separation of electromagnetic polarizations.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown with Figure 9.1: a ring of particles around a central one is deformed into ellipses that alternate orientation every half cycle; Exercises 9.13-9.16 make the 45-degree rotation and orthogonality precise.
concepts.notes: The book uses the symbol h_+ (Eq. 9.58) and the words '+' and 'x' polarization in the Figure 9.1 caption; it does not introduce a separate h_x symbol.

concepts.name: TT coordinates and free particles
aliases: free particles remain at rest in TT gauge
concepts.definition: In TT gauge adapted to a particle's initial rest frame, Gamma^alpha_00 vanishes identically, so a free particle initially at rest keeps constant coordinates as the wave passes. The coordinates simply follow free particles; constancy of coordinate position therefore carries no invariant information about the wave.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from the geodesic equation by evaluating the initial acceleration, then iterating the argument in time; immediately flagged as a coordinate statement so the reader does not conclude the wave has no effect.

concepts.name: proper-distance strain
concepts.definition: The fractional change of the proper distance between free particles caused by a wave: for particles on the x axis at coordinate separation epsilon, Delta l = (1 + h_xx^TT/2) epsilon to first order. The change is proportional to the separation and to amplitudes of order 1e-21 or less, which is why detectors are kilometres long.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed directly by integrating sqrt(g_xx) between the two coordinate-fixed particles; used as the first invariant evidence that the wave is physical.

concepts.name: geodesic deviation in a gravitational wave
aliases: Riemann tensor as measurable tidal field
tidal acceleration of a gravitational wave
concepts.definition: In a local inertial frame attached to one freely falling particle, the proper components of the separation vector to a nearby free particle obey d^2 xi^j/dt^2 = -R^j_{0k0} xi^k, with R_{x0x0} = -h_xx,00^TT/2, R_{y0x0} = -h_xy,00^TT/2 and R_{y0y0} = -R_{x0x0} for a wave along z. The Riemann tensor is thus measurable by watching separations of nearby geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the need for coordinates tied to measurement: in the local inertial frame the second covariant derivative along the geodesic becomes an ordinary second derivative, and the four-velocity can be taken at zeroth order because R is already first order.
prerequisites: gauge invariance of the linearized Riemann tensor

concepts.name: gauge invariance of the linearized Riemann tensor
aliases: Riemann tensor unchanged by infinitesimal coordinate changes
concepts.definition: Under the gauge transformations of linearized theory the first-order Riemann tensor does not change, so its components computed in TT gauge equal those in a local inertial frame; statements expressed through R and proper lengths are therefore gauge-free.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to justify evaluating R in the simple TT gauge while interpreting the deviation equation in the local inertial frame, and to reinterpret xi^alpha as proper lengths.
concepts.notes: Exercise 9.10 illustrates this with two metrics differing by a gauge transformation that give identical curvature.

concepts.name: tidal force of a gravitational wave
concepts.definition: The effective force per unit mass -R^i_{0j0} xi^j that a wave exerts on one body relative to a freely falling reference body, measured in the reference body's local inertial frame. Being a force, it adds to non-gravitational forces, so relative motion obeys xi-double-dot = -R xi + F_B/m_B - F_A/m_A.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the advantage of the differential (deviation) form over the integrated proper-distance form: only the former can include springs, electric binding or friction.
prerequisites: geodesic deviation in a gravitational wave

concepts.name: stretching of space and rigid rulers
concepts.definition: Saying a wave 'stretches space' means proper separations of free bodies change. A solid ruler does not follow this because interatomic electromagnetic forces enormously exceed the tidal force of the wave, so its length hardly changes and it can be used to record the free masses' tidal displacements.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as a common student question (a ruler is mostly empty space, so why would it not stretch too?) and answered with the forced deviation equation; followed by the preferable alternative of timing light between the free masses.
prerequisites: tidal force of a gravitational wave

concepts.name: circular and elliptical polarization
concepts.definition: Complex superpositions of the two linear states. Circular polarization has h_yy^TT = -h_xx^TT and h_xy^TT = +/- i h_xx^TT, so the two components oscillate a quarter cycle apart and the deformation ellipse rotates without changing shape; the general case with h_xy = alpha h_xx is elliptical about suitable axes, with linear and circular as special cases.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in Exercise 9.15 and used in §9.4, where the factor i in the binary's h_xy makes radiation along the orbital axis circularly polarized and radiation in the orbital plane linearly polarized; intermediate inclinations give ellipticity that encodes the inclination.

concepts.name: exact plane wave (pp-wave)
concepts.definition: An exact vacuum solution ds^2 = -du dv + f(u)^2 dx^2 + g(u)^2 dy^2 with u = t - z, whose only field equation is f''/f + g''/g = 0; one function may be chosen freely, as in the linear waveform. For g = 1 + epsilon(u) with small epsilon, f is approximately 1 - epsilon(u), reproducing a linear plus-polarized wave, and particles at rest in these coordinates stay at rest.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by asking whether the linear wave survives in the full nonlinear theory; built by guessing a metric that depends only on retarded time and stretches only transverse directions, then computing Christoffel symbols and Riemann components.
concepts.notes: References: Ehlers and Kundt (1962) §2.5; Stephani et al. (2004) §24.5. See gaps for printed slips in the Christoffel list.

concepts.name: null coordinates
aliases: u = t - z, v = t + z
concepts.definition: Coordinates u = t - z and v = t + z that label outgoing and ingoing light rays along z; the flat line element becomes -du dv + dx^2 + dy^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Reintroduced from Exercise 3.34 because the sought exact wave should depend only on u.

concepts.name: geometrical optics for gravitational waves
concepts.definition: When a wave's wavelength is short compared with the curvature radius of the background and its period short compared with the timescale of background change, it travels along null geodesics of the background and parallel-transports its polarization tensor, exactly as light does. Unlike light it is almost unaffected by intervening matter, because its coupling is as weak as its effect on matter.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as the practical question of how waves reach us through the fields of stars and galaxies; answered qualitatively by analogy with electromagnetic waves in media, without derivation.

concepts.name: gravitational lensing
concepts.definition: Convergence of neighbouring null geodesics that focuses and amplifies waves (gravitational or electromagnetic) passing near masses.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in passing as a consequence of geometrical-optics propagation, with a forward pointer to Chapter 11.

concepts.name: gravitational-wave spectrum and detector bands
concepts.definition: The span of gravitational-wave frequencies and matching detection methods: roughly 10 Hz to a few kHz for ground interferometers and bars, 0.01-10 Hz decihertz band for proposed missions, millihertz for LISA, below 0.1 mHz for spacecraft tracking, nanohertz for pulsar timing, and about 1e-16 Hz for primordial waves imprinted on CMB polarization. Ground detectors cannot go below about 1 Hz because fluctuating Newtonian gravity of the Earth dominates.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by analogy with the history of multiwavelength astronomy, then organized as a list of detector families with their physical limits.

concepts.name: resonant bar detector
concepts.definition: A massive elastic body, idealized as two masses joined by a damped spring, whose vibrational mode is driven by the wave's tidal force. Its stretch obeys a forced damped oscillator equation with driving term l_0 h_xx,00^TT/2, so the response is largest on resonance and grows with Q. Bars never reached the needed sensitivity or bandwidth and have been retired.
concepts.how_introduced: Studied as a case study of waves acting on matter: the spring force is written in terms of proper length, Newton's law is applied in a local inertial frame that coincides with TT coordinates to first order, and the coordinate separation is eliminated.
prerequisites: tidal force of a gravitational wave

concepts.name: quality factor
concepts.definition: For a damped oscillator, Q = omega_0/(2 gamma), where 1/Q is the average fraction of stored energy of the free oscillator lost per radian of oscillation. A resonant detector's amplitude grows like Q and its energy like Q^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined when simplifying the resonant energy of the bar; derivation from the energy-loss definition is left to Exercise 9.25. Returns for mirror suspensions, where very high Q confines thermal noise to narrow bands.

concepts.name: thermal noise
concepts.definition: Random excitation of each mechanical mode of a detector with mean energy k_B T. It competes with the energy deposited by a wave, forcing cryogenic bars (to 3 K and below 100 mK) and, in interferometers, ultra-high-Q mirrors and suspensions that push the noise into narrow resonances outside the observation band.
concepts.how_introduced: Estimated by comparing k_B T at room temperature with the energy a strong resonant wave would give a Weber bar, then extended to interferometer mirrors.

concepts.name: seismic isolation
concepts.definition: Protecting test masses from ground motion by hanging them as chains of low-frequency pendulums, which transmit little motion above their resonance, supplemented by absorbing mounts, active cancellation driven by seismometers, and in KAGRA's case underground siting.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained for bars and carried over to interferometer mirrors; compared to noise-cancelling headphones.

concepts.name: quantum limit and squeezed light
concepts.definition: At very small excitations the measurement is limited by quantum mechanics: for a bar the deposited energy falls below one phonon of the mode; for interferometers photon-number and radiation-pressure fluctuations set a standard quantum limit. Quantum nondemolition techniques and squeezed light manipulate uncertainty to measure below it, and LIGO and Virgo now use squeezing.
concepts.how_introduced: Brought up as the second obstacle bars faced when aiming at 1e-21 bursts, with pointers to the literature; the bibliography adds the history of quantum nondemolition ideas.

concepts.name: radar ranging of proper distance
concepts.definition: Measuring distance by timing a light signal's round trip on the sender's clock. For separations small compared with the gravitational wavelength it gives the proper distance even in a wave spacetime; in TT coordinates the photon's coordinate speed along x is (1 + h_+)^{-1/2}, which does not conflict with relativity because proper time, not coordinate speed, is measured.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the foundation of beam detectors: compute the return time by integrating the effective coordinate speed, using the unperturbed path inside h_+ to first order.

concepts.name: return-time response of a beam detector
concepts.definition: For a plus wave travelling perpendicular to an arm of coordinate length L, the rate of change of round-trip time with emission time is 1 + [h_+(t_start + 2L) - h_+(t_start)]/2, so only the wave at emission and at reception matters; this ratio is also the frequency ratio of returned to emitted light. For a wave at angle theta to the arm's normal a third term, evaluated at the reflection time, appears.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by differentiating the integral expression for the return time with respect to the start time, turning the integral of a derivative back into the function; the oblique case is quoted and left to Exercise 9.27.

concepts.name: beam detectors
concepts.definition: Detectors that sense gravitational waves through their effect on arrival times of electromagnetic signals exchanged between free masses: Doppler tracking of interplanetary spacecraft, pulsar timing arrays, and laser interferometers. Single-beam versions are limited by clock stability and propagation noise.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with spacecraft tracking; the three-term signature is used to separate a real wave from plasma fluctuations; clock stability of order 1e-19 rules out amplitudes near 1e-20, motivating interferometers.
prerequisites: return-time response of a beam detector

concepts.name: laser interferometer detector
concepts.definition: A detector that splits stable laser light into two perpendicular arms ending on suspended, effectively free mirrors, and recombines the returning beams so that the output at the dark port tracks the difference of round-trip times. It acts as two beam detectors in which each arm is the clock for the other; a plus wave arriving along the normal stretches one arm while shrinking the other, a cross wave from the same direction gives no signal, and the response is broadband with an antenna pattern covering most of the sky.
concepts.how_introduced: Built conceptually from the beam-detector formula and the ring-of-particles picture (place arms along x and y in Figure 9.1), then described in hardware terms for LIGO and Virgo.
prerequisites: return-time response of a beam detector

concepts.name: Fabry-Perot arm cavities and power recycling
concepts.definition: Placing a nearly fully reflecting mirror near the beamsplitter in each arm so light bounces many times, lengthening the effective storage time and building up power; and adding a recycling mirror that returns the bright-port light to the interferometer in phase with fresh laser light.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained as the practical equivalent of folding the beam many times, with the optical layout shown in Figure 9.3.

concepts.name: shot noise
concepts.definition: Random fluctuations in detected light power arising from the discreteness of photons; a quantum noise that limits interferometer sensitivity above roughly 200 Hz and whose fractional size decreases as the stored light power increases.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as the last major noise source, completing a picture in which seismic noise limits low frequencies, thermal noise the middle band, and shot noise high frequencies, yielding a 20 Hz-2 kHz band.

concepts.name: detector network localization
concepts.definition: Combining several detectors to confirm events and extract what one detector cannot: the arrival-time delay between two sites separated by d lies within +/- d/c and restricts the source to a ring on the sky, a third detector narrows it to two patches, and non-aligned detectors measure both polarizations and hence the binary inclination.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the single-output nature of an interferometer and by confidence requirements; described with LIGO Hanford, Livingston, Virgo, KAGRA and LIGO-India.

concepts.name: LISA
concepts.definition: A planned ESA mission with NASA participation: three drag-free spacecraft in an equilateral triangle with 2.5e6 km arms, orbiting the Sun at 1 AU about 20 degrees behind the Earth, forming effectively three 60-degree interferometers that measure both polarizations in the millihertz band, sensitive to massive black hole mergers of 1e4-1e7 solar masses throughout the Universe. Because its sources stay in band for months, LISA locates them on the sky from the frequency and amplitude modulation produced by its annual orbit around the Sun.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the answer to the terrestrial gravity-noise wall below 1 Hz, including its transponded (not reflected) beams, time-delay interferometry, and position finding from orbital modulation.

concepts.name: time-delay interferometry
concepts.definition: Constructing interferometric observables in data analysis by combining phase measurements of separate one-way laser links recorded at appropriately delayed times, used when arms are long, unequal and changing so that light cannot be simply recombined at a beamsplitter.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the LISA description with a pointer to Tinto and Dhurandhar (2014).

concepts.name: drag-free operation
concepts.definition: Keeping test masses in near-perfect free fall inside a spacecraft that shields them from solar radiation pressure and solar wind and uses tiny thrusters to follow the masses without touching them; demonstrated beyond LISA requirements by LISA Pathfinder.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained as LISA's counterpart of seismic isolation.

concepts.name: cosmic sound analogy
concepts.definition: Gravitational-wave detection resembles acoustics more than optical astronomy: detectors follow the phase of low-frequency waves, cannot focus on a small patch of sky and so have broad quadrupolar antenna patterns, locate sources by phase delays across arrays, and receive waves generated coherently by bulk mass motions (as sound is by pressure changes) rather than by incoherent atomic emission.
concepts.how_introduced: Closing subsection of §9.3; the coherence of emission is tied to gravity having only one sign of 'charge'; the language of chirps and sirens is explained.

concepts.name: slow-motion approximation
concepts.definition: The assumption that the source region is much smaller than the gravitational wavelength 2 pi/Omega, equivalently that internal velocities are much less than c, so that retardation across the source can be neglected and the leading radiation is quadrupolar.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as one of two assumptions (sinusoidal time dependence and small size) before solving the sourced wave equation; argued to hold for all but the most powerful sources.

concepts.name: outgoing spherical wave
aliases: retarded monopole solution of the Helmholtz equation
concepts.definition: The spherically symmetric vacuum solution B = A e^{i Omega r}/r of the Helmholtz equation, which with e^{-i Omega t} describes waves travelling away from the source with amplitude falling as 1/r; the ingoing e^{-i Omega r} solution is discarded by the choice of boundary condition.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted as the dominant slow-motion solution outside the source, with the separation-of-variables and Bessel-function justification in Exercise 9.29.

concepts.name: quadrupole moment tensor
aliases: second moment of the mass distribution
concepts.definition: The tensor I^{lm} = integral of T^00 x^l x^m d^3x, the second moment of the energy (for slow sources, mass) distribution about the origin, defined without removing the trace and without a factor of 3 (the MTW convention).
concepts.how_introduced: Emerges when the tensor virial identity rewrites the integrated stresses J_ij as half the second time derivative of this integral.
concepts.notes: The book warns conventions differ between texts; many use a trace-free version with a factor 3.

concepts.name: tensor virial identity
concepts.definition: For a conserved stress-energy tensor with compact support, the second time derivative of the integral of T^00 x^l x^m equals twice the integral of T^lm, linking internal stresses to the changing mass quadrupole.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without proof (with a mis-numbered exercise pointer) to convert the spatial source integral J_ij into the second time derivative of a mass moment.
concepts.notes: The text attributes this identity to 'Exercise 9.24', but Exercise 9.24 in this chapter asks for Eq. 9.53; the pointer is a cross-reference slip, and the identity itself follows from T^{mu nu}_{,nu} = 0 by two integrations by parts.

concepts.name: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation
aliases: no monopole or dipole gravitational waves
concepts.definition: Because T^{mu nu}_{,nu} = 0, the total energy and momentum of an isolated source are constant, so the 1/r parts of h-bar^{mu 0} are time independent and carry no wave; the leading wave field comes from the time-varying mass quadrupole. This parallels the way charge conservation forbids electromagnetic monopole radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived for a sinusoidal source by differentiating J^{mu 0} in time, using the conservation law and Gauss's theorem on a surface outside the source; later generalized to arbitrary time dependence with the retarded integral.

concepts.name: quadrupole approximation
aliases: quadrupole formula for the wave field
concepts.definition: The far-zone, slow-motion wave field h-bar_jk = (2/r) d^2 I_jk/dt^2 evaluated at retarded time t - r (for a sinusoidal source, -2 Omega^2 D_jk e^{i Omega (r - t)}/r), neglecting 1/r^2 terms and 1/r terms of higher order in source velocity.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled from the ball-integration result h-bar = 4J e^{i Omega (r-t)}/r, the vanishing of J^{mu 0}, and the tensor virial identity; justified for Newtonian-gravity-bound sources only by reference to the literature.
prerequisites: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation
concepts.notes: Signs as printed in Eqs. 9.83 and 9.106 are not mutually consistent; see gaps_and_pitfalls.

concepts.name: reduced quadrupole moment
concepts.definition: The trace-free part of the mass quadrupole, I-slash_jk = I_jk - (1/3) delta_jk I^l_l. The TT wave field and the radiated power depend only on it, so spherically symmetric mass distributions (with I proportional to delta) do not contribute.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears when the quadrupole field is put into TT gauge along the propagation direction.
concepts.notes: Printed as an I with a horizontal bar through it; rendered here as calligraphic I.

concepts.name: TT projection of spherical waves
concepts.definition: Converting a Lorenz-gauge radiation field into TT gauge for propagation direction n by projecting transversely with P_ij = delta_ij - n_i n_j and removing the transverse trace: h^TT_ij = P_i^k P_j^l h-bar_kl - (1/2) P_ij P^kl h-bar_kl. For n along z this gives h_xx^TT = (h-bar_xx - h-bar_yy)/2 and h_xy^TT = h-bar_xy.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as possible (Exercise 9.32) and applied along z; the projector form is given in Exercise 9.33 and used to obtain radiation in arbitrary directions.

concepts.name: orbital inclination
concepts.definition: The angle iota between the normal to a binary's orbital plane and the line of sight. The plus amplitude scales as (1 + cos^2 iota) and the cross amplitude as 2 cos iota, so a face-on orbit emits circularly polarized waves toward us and an edge-on orbit linearly polarized waves; the ratio of polarizations measures iota, which must be known to convert amplitude into distance.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the general-inclination binary formula (derived in Exercise 9.38) and used in the network and standard-siren discussions.

concepts.name: order-of-magnitude wave amplitude
concepts.definition: A source of mass M, size R and internal speed v produces h of order M v^2/r at distance r; for self-gravitating motion v^2 ~ phi_0 (the internal potential), so h ~ phi_0 phi_r with phi_r = M/r, and the absolute ceiling for fully relativistic sources is about M/r.
concepts.how_introduced: First as a crude ceiling at the start of §9.4 (metric perturbation of order 1 at distance M, falling as 1/r), then from D_jk ~ M R^2 in the quadrupole field combined with the virial theorem.
concepts.notes: Also shows the wave tidal force exceeds the static Newtonian tidal force by (phi_0 r/R)^2 and that the Newtonian description of a dynamic source's field fails beyond r ~ R/phi_0.

concepts.name: no gravitational radiation from spherically symmetric motion
concepts.definition: Purely spherically symmetric mass motions emit no gravitational waves at any order. In the quadrupole approximation this follows because the quadrupole of a spherical distribution is proportional to delta_jk and its trace-free part vanishes; the full statement follows from Birkhoff's theorem, and in linear theory from the retarded integral.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a reason the amplitude estimate is optimistic for realistic collapses; the caution that a leading-order argument is not a proof leads to the example of a rotating square of four masses, which has constant quadrupole yet radiates at higher order.
prerequisites: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation

concepts.name: retarded solution
concepts.definition: The outgoing solution of the sourced wave equation, h-bar_mu nu(t, x) = 4 times the integral of T_mu nu(t - |x - y|, y)/|x - y| over the source, i.e. an integral over the past light cone; far away it reduces to (4/r) times the source integral at retarded time t - r.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from standard wave theory as the exact solution that generalizes the sinusoidal treatment to arbitrary time dependence.

concepts.name: Feynman sticky-bead argument
concepts.definition: Feynman's 1957 argument that gravitational waves carry energy: if tidal motion of beads on a rod with friction produces heat, the energy must come from the wave. Schutz turns it into a calculation by replacing beads with damped oscillators and assuming energy conservation.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to motivate §9.5 and credited in the bibliography to the Chapel Hill conference; the oscillators later drop out of the flux formula.
prerequisites: tidal force of a gravitational wave

concepts.name: energy flux of a gravitational wave
concepts.definition: The period-averaged energy crossing unit area per unit time, F = Omega^2 A^2/(32 pi) for a linearly polarized plane wave of amplitude A, or F = Omega^2 <h^TT_mu nu h^TT mu nu>/(32 pi); in general (1/32 pi) times the average of the squared time derivatives summed over TT components. It is invariant under background Lorentz transformations but not under gauge changes, and is meaningful only in linearized theory as an average.
concepts.how_introduced: Fixed by demanding that the power absorbed by a sheet of oscillators equals the loss of flux implied by the reduced downstream amplitude; the ratio dF/dA contains no oscillator properties.

concepts.name: radiation reaction by destructive interference
concepts.definition: A detector driven by a wave also radiates; the portion emitted straight downstream has the incident frequency and a phase such that it interferes destructively with the incident wave, reducing its amplitude by exactly the amount that accounts for the energy the detector absorbs. Emission in other directions cancels among neighbouring oscillators in a plane array.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by noticing the inconsistency of treating the detector as a test body, pictured in Figures 9.5-9.6, and computed by summing quadrupole fields over a plane with a convergence factor (footnote 4 explains why only the downstream direction matters).

concepts.name: quadrupole luminosity formula
concepts.definition: The total power radiated by a slow-motion source, L = (1/5) <third time derivative of I-slash_ij times that of I-slash^ij> in geometrized units (G/5c^5 in SI), reducing to L = (1/5) Omega^6 <I-slash_ij I-slash^ij> for sinusoidal motion.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by writing the flux on the z axis in terms of the reduced quadrupole, replacing the z direction by the radial unit vector, and integrating over a sphere using the symmetric angular averages of n^i n^j and n^i n^j n^k n^l.
prerequisites: energy flux of a gravitational wave
concepts.notes: Order of magnitude L ~ phi_0^2 v^6, at most ~phi_0^5.

concepts.name: maximum luminosity c^5/G
concepts.definition: No source can radiate much more than c^5/G, about 3.6e52 W (luminosity 1 in geometrized units): radiation of luminosity L crossing a region of size R contains energy of order LR, whose own Newtonian potential is of order L, and a potential well above 1 would form a black hole trapping the radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained first from scaling of the quadrupole formula, then justified by the energy-of-radiation argument, and compared with quasars and gamma-ray bursts (below 1e-10) and black hole mergers (about 1e-3 to 1e-2).

concepts.name: Isaacson stress-energy tensor
concepts.definition: The averaged tensor T_alpha beta = <<h^TT_mu nu,alpha h^TT mu nu_,beta>>/(32 pi), with averages over several periods and wavelengths, which assigns energy and momentum to a gravitational wave packet; its T^{0z} reproduces the plane-wave flux.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only in Exercise 9.50, with a pointer to MTW; Exercise 9.54 uses it for angular momentum loss.
prerequisites: energy flux of a gravitational wave

concepts.name: localization of gravitational energy
concepts.definition: In general relativity the energy of the gravitational field cannot be assigned to points in a coordinate-independent way; near flat spacetime and to lowest order in h, averaged conserved quantities can be defined, and the wave flux is the unique expression consistent with energy conservation at that order.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as an objection a careful reader would make, recalling §7.3; Schutz turns the derivation around to argue the constructed flux is the only acceptable definition within linear theory.
prerequisites: energy flux of a gravitational wave

concepts.name: orbital decay by gravitational radiation
aliases: period decrease of a radiating binary
concepts.definition: A bound binary that loses energy at rate L becomes more tightly bound, speeding up and shortening its period: for a circular Newtonian orbit dP/dt = 3PL/(2E), a dimensionless number independent of units. The effect has been measured for binary pulsars in agreement with general relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as how long radiation takes to change the orbit; obtained by logarithmic differentiation of E(omega) and dE/dt = -L.

concepts.name: Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar
concepts.definition: A double neutron star system containing a radio pulsar, discovered in 1974, with orbital period about 7 h 45 min, eccentricity 0.617 and component masses near 1.4 solar masses. The measured decrease of its orbital period, -(2.398 +/- 0.004)e-12, matches the quadrupole-formula prediction -2.40263e-12 to 0.17 percent, the first strong (indirect) evidence for gravitational radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the opening Nobel-prize framing, used for the amplitude estimate in §9.4, and analyzed quantitatively at the end of §9.5.

concepts.name: geometrized units
concepts.definition: Units with G = c = 1 in which masses and times are lengths (1.4 solar masses is 2.07 km; the Hulse-Taylor period is 8.37e12 m) and luminosity is dimensionless, with conversion factor c^5/G = 3.63e52 W.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited with the advice to do calculations in these units and convert only at the end, illustrated by the binary luminosity.

concepts.name: chirp mass
concepts.definition: The combination M_chirp = mu^{3/5} M^{2/5} = (m1 m2)^{3/5}/(m1 + m2)^{1/5} of a binary's masses, the only mass parameter that enters the leading-order gravitational waveform amplitude, luminosity and frequency evolution; it can be read from the signal through omega and its time derivative.
concepts.how_introduced: Discovered by rewriting unequal-mass amplitudes: they depend only on mu M^{2/3}, which motivates the definition; named for its role in the frequency sweep.
concepts.notes: The Newtonian energy is also a function of the chirp mass alone, yet the quantity only became important through gravitational-wave physics.

concepts.name: scale-free nature of gravity
aliases: absence of intrinsic scale in general relativity
concepts.definition: Vacuum general relativity in geometrized units contains no preferred mass, length or time, so a binary with all masses multiplied by a factor produces the same waveform stretched in time by that factor and the same amplitude at a distance scaled by that factor; every dimensionless quantity of a circular inspiral depends only on the product of chirp mass and orbital frequency.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced at the start of §9.6 and demonstrated by writing amplitudes, luminosity, energy and phase in terms of chirp mass and (M omega).

concepts.name: chirp time
concepts.definition: The instantaneous timescale omega/omega-dot on which a binary's orbital frequency changes by order unity: (5/96) M_chirp (M_chirp omega)^{-8/3}, shrinking rapidly as the orbit tightens.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from the chirp-mass form of energy balance; named after the rising-frequency 'chirp' of the signal.

concepts.name: time to merger
concepts.definition: The remaining lifetime of a point-mass circular binary from orbital frequency omega until the frequency formally diverges, (5/256) M_chirp (M_chirp omega)^{-8/3}, which is 3/8 of the chirp time because the decay accelerates.
concepts.how_introduced: Integrate dt/d omega from the present frequency to infinity (Exercise 9.43).

concepts.name: remaining orbital phase and mass-independent luminosity
concepts.definition: The orbital phase still to accumulate before merger is psi_merger = (1/32)(M_chirp omega)^{-5/3}, and eliminating (M_chirp omega) gives L = 1/(160 psi_merger^2): a circular binary's gravitational luminosity depends only on how many orbits it has left, whatever its masses.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the dimensionless nature of phase; credited to Forward and Berman (1967). Consequences: all merging black hole pairs reach similar peak luminosity near 0.01, and all radiate the same fraction of their mass-energy.

concepts.name: standard siren
concepts.definition: A source whose intrinsic gravitational-wave luminosity can be inferred from its own signal, so that the measured amplitude yields its distance. For an inspiralling binary, omega and omega-dot give the chirp mass, polarization gives the inclination, and then r = alpha M_chirp (M_chirp omega)^{2/3}/h with alpha of order 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Framed by analogy with astronomers' standard candles and the sound vocabulary of the field; history traced from Forward and Berman's implicit result to Schutz (1986).

concepts.name: luminosity distance
concepts.definition: The distance d_L defined by L = 4 pi d_L^2 F for a source of known luminosity; for receding or cosmologically distant sources it absorbs redshift factors and, in cosmology, the effects of spatial curvature, and it is the distance a standard siren measures.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced when redshift is found to multiply the inferred siren distance by (1 + z), with deferral to Chapter 13.

concepts.name: redshifted chirp mass
concepts.definition: Because a detector measures only times, a source moving away with redshift z shows frequency and frequency drift reduced as if its chirp mass were (1 + z) times larger; the same holds for component masses, so gravitational waves alone cannot separate mass from redshift.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by inspection of the chirp-mass formula once one notes that all binary observables are time measurements affected by redshift.

concepts.name: circularization by gravitational radiation
concepts.definition: Gravitational-wave emission reduces orbital eccentricity faster than it shrinks the semi-major axis (de/dt is proportional to e/a^4 while da/dt scales as 1/a^3), so binaries observed late in their inspiral by ground detectors are nearly circular; the Hulse-Taylor system will have e below 1e-5 when it reaches the LIGO band.
concepts.how_introduced: Discussed at the end of §9.6 using the Peters-Mathews averages from Exercise 9.56.

concepts.name: post-Newtonian corrections
concepts.definition: Corrections to Newtonian orbital motion and to the waveform in powers of v/c that grow as a binary tightens; they break the chirp-mass degeneracy and allow the individual masses to be measured, though less precisely than the chirp mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the limitation of the chapter's Newtonian-orbit model, with references to Blanchet, Poisson and Will, and Andersson.

concepts.name: cosmological gravitational-wave background
aliases: stochastic background from the Big Bang
concepts.definition: A random, statistically superposed field of gravitational waves left over from the very early Universe, expected to have a roughly flat spectrum across frequencies and very small present-day amplitude. Waves present when the microwave background was released would have imprinted a polarization pattern on it; detecting either the waves or that imprint would probe physics at energies far beyond accelerators.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among detection strategies (CMB polarization) in the survey of detector families, with the remark that such waves may date from about 1e-25 s after the Big Bang and that their frequencies today are around 1e-16 Hz; the physics is deferred to Chapter 13.
concepts.notes: Pulsar timing arrays and LISA also target stochastic backgrounds, though the book's discussion of those is in Chapter 12.

key_equations.name: Vacuum linearized field equation
key_equations.meaning: Far from sources and in Lorenz gauge, every component of the trace-reversed perturbation obeys the flat-space wave equation.
key_equations.symbols: h-bar^{alpha beta}: trace-reversed metric perturbation; c = 1.

key_equations.name: Plane-wave ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Trial solution with constant complex amplitude and constant real wave one-form; physical field is the real part.
key_equations.symbols: A^{alpha beta}: amplitude tensor; k_alpha: wave one-form.

key_equations.name: Wave operator on a plane wave
key_equations.meaning: Each derivative of the exponential brings down i k, so the wave equation becomes algebraic.

key_equations.name: Null wave vector
key_equations.meaning: The plane wave solves the vacuum equation only if k is null: gravitational waves move at the speed of light.

key_equations.name: Phase surfaces and frequency
key_equations.latex: k_\alpha x^\alpha=k_0t+\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x={\rm const},\qquad \vec k\to(\omega,\mathbf k)
key_equations.meaning: Wave fronts are hypersurfaces of constant phase; the time component of k is the angular frequency.
key_equations.symbols: omega = k^0

key_equations.name: Photon rides the wave
key_equations.meaning: A photon moving along k keeps constant wave phase because k.k = 0.
key_equations.symbols: lambda: affine parameter; l^mu: initial position.

key_equations.name: Dispersion relation
key_equations.meaning: Phase and group velocity both equal 1; no dispersion.

key_equations.name: Lorenz gauge and transversality to k
key_equations.meaning: The gauge condition needed for Eq. 9.1 makes the amplitude orthogonal to the wave vector.

key_equations.name: Residual gauge generator
key_equations.meaning: Gauge vectors that solve the wave equation preserve Lorenz gauge; a plane-wave choice with the same k is used.
key_equations.symbols: B_alpha: constant complex vector.

key_equations.name: Gauge change of h and h-bar
key_equations.meaning: How the perturbation and its trace-reversed form change under an infinitesimal coordinate transformation.

key_equations.name: Gauge change of the amplitude
key_equations.latex: A^{(\rm NEW)}_{\alpha\beta}=A^{(\rm OLD)}_{\alpha\beta}-iB_\alpha k_\beta-iB_\beta k_\alpha+i\eta_{\alpha\beta}B^\mu k_\mu
key_equations.meaning: After dividing out the exponential, the gauge change is algebraic in B, which can be tuned to impose further conditions.

key_equations.name: TT conditions
key_equations.meaning: Traceless and orthogonal to a chosen constant four-velocity; with Eq. 9.12 these define transverse-traceless gauge.
key_equations.symbols: U^beta: fixed timelike unit vector.

key_equations.name: TT perturbation equals its trace reverse
key_equations.meaning: Tracelessness makes the bar operation trivial.

key_equations.name: TT amplitude matrix for a wave along z
key_equations.meaning: Only two independent physical amplitudes remain: the plus and cross polarizations.

key_equations.name: Initial acceleration of a free particle in TT gauge
key_equations.meaning: Vanishes because all h_{beta 0}^TT are zero, so particles initially at rest keep fixed TT coordinates.

key_equations.name: Proper separation of free particles
key_equations.meaning: The invariant distance between coordinate-fixed free particles oscillates with the wave, by a fraction h/2, proportional to the separation.
key_equations.symbols: epsilon: coordinate separation along x.

key_equations.name: Geodesic deviation in a local inertial frame
key_equations.meaning: In a local inertial frame Christoffel symbols vanish at the point, so the covariant second derivative is an ordinary one.
key_equations.symbols: xi: connecting vector; U: four-velocity of the particles.

key_equations.name: Tidal acceleration from curvature
key_equations.meaning: With U = (1,0,0,0) and xi = (0, epsilon, 0, 0) to lowest order, the Riemann tensor is measured directly by relative accelerations.

key_equations.name: Riemann components of a plane wave in TT gauge
key_equations.meaning: All other independent components vanish; the curvature is the second time derivative of the TT strain.

key_equations.label: (9.28a)
key_equations.name: Motion of an x-separated pair
key_equations.meaning: Plus polarization moves the partner along the separation; cross polarization moves it sideways. Consistent with Eq. 9.24.

key_equations.label: (9.28b)
key_equations.name: Motion of a y-separated pair
key_equations.meaning: The y direction responds with opposite sign to the x direction under plus polarization.

key_equations.name: Tidal acceleration law
key_equations.meaning: The wave acts on particle B like a force proportional to its separation from freely falling particle A.

key_equations.name: Tidal force plus other forces
key_equations.meaning: Non-gravitational forces add to the wave's tidal term, allowing treatment of bound systems such as rulers and bars.
key_equations.symbols: F_A, F_B: non-gravitational forces on particles of masses m_A, m_B.

key_equations.name: Exact plane-wave metric and curvature
key_equations.meaning: A nonlinear wave depending only on retarded time u = t - z; dots are u-derivatives. The book also lists Gamma^v_xx as 2 f-dot/f; for this metric it is 2 f f-dot.
key_equations.symbols: u = t - z, v = t + z.

key_equations.name: Vacuum equation for the exact plane wave
key_equations.meaning: One free function (the waveform) remains; for g = 1 + epsilon(u), f is approximately 1 - epsilon(u), the linear plus wave.

key_equations.name: Free damped oscillator
key_equations.meaning: Two masses on a damped spring in flat spacetime.
key_equations.symbols: k: spring constant; nu: damping constant; l_0: natural length.

key_equations.name: Proper length of the spring in the wave
key_equations.meaning: The spring responds to proper, not coordinate, extension.

key_equations.name: Bar detector equation
key_equations.meaning: The physical stretch is a forced damped oscillator driven by the wave's tidal acceleration.
key_equations.symbols: xi = l - l_0: proper stretch.

key_equations.name: Steady response to a sinusoidal wave
key_equations.meaning: Standard driven-oscillator amplitude and phase, with transients decaying on 1/gamma.

key_equations.name: Mean oscillation energy
key_equations.meaning: Time-averaged energy of the driven detector.
key_equations.symbols: angle brackets: average over a period.

key_equations.name: Resonant amplitude and quality factor
key_equations.meaning: On resonance the stretch is enhanced by the ratio Omega/gamma, i.e. by 2Q.

key_equations.name: Resonant energy deposited
key_equations.meaning: Energy a wave pumps into a resonant detector; its existence suggests waves carry energy.

key_equations.name: Plus-polarized wave metric (TT)
key_equations.meaning: Starting metric for radar ranging between free masses. Printed with h_+(z - t) in the dx^2 term and h_+(t - z) in the dy^2 term; a single argument t - z is used here.
key_equations.symbols: h_+: plus amplitude as a function of retarded time.

key_equations.name: Coordinate speed of light along x
key_equations.meaning: A coordinate speed, not a violation of relativity.

key_equations.name: Round-trip time
key_equations.meaning: First-order light travel time out and back, obtained by using the unperturbed path inside h_+; t is proper time for the free masses.
key_equations.symbols: L: coordinate arm length.

key_equations.name: Rate of change of return time
key_equations.meaning: Only the wave at emission and reception matters for a wave travelling perpendicular to the arm; equals nu_return/nu_start.

key_equations.name: Three-term beam-detector response
key_equations.meaning: Tilting the propagation direction by theta away from z (staying in the x-z plane) makes the field at the moment of reflection contribute as well; this three-appearance signature underlies noise rejection in spacecraft tracking.
key_equations.symbols: theta: angle between propagation direction and the z axis.

key_equations.name: Sourced linearized field equation
key_equations.meaning: Wave equation with matter source, to be solved in the slow-motion approximation.

key_equations.name: Sinusoidal source reduces to Helmholtz equation
key_equations.meaning: Time dependence factored out component by component.

key_equations.name: Vacuum spherical solutions
key_equations.meaning: Outgoing and ingoing waves; Z = 0 for emission.

key_equations.name: Integrating over a small source ball
key_equations.meaning: The Omega^2 term is negligible for a small source; Gauss's theorem turns the Laplacian into a flux fixed by the exterior solution.
key_equations.symbols: epsilon: source radius, much less than 2 pi/Omega.

key_equations.name: Field of a compact oscillating source
key_equations.meaning: Leading far-field radiation in terms of the integrated source.

key_equations.name: Conservation kills time-dependent J^{mu 0}
key_equations.latex: i\Omega J^{\mu0}e^{-i\Omega t}=\int T^{\mu k}{}_{,k}d^3x=\oint T^{\mu k}n_k\,dS=0\ \Rightarrow\ J^{\mu0}=0,\ \bar h^{\mu0}=0
key_equations.meaning: Energy-momentum conservation means the monopole and momentum parts carry no oscillating field.

key_equations.name: Tensor virial identity
key_equations.meaning: Integrated stresses equal half the second time derivative of the mass quadrupole.

key_equations.label: (9.82a)-(9.82b)
key_equations.name: Quadrupole moment tensor
key_equations.meaning: Second mass moment (MTW convention, trace not removed).
key_equations.symbols: D^{lm}: complex amplitude of the quadrupole.

key_equations.name: Quadrupole wave field (Lorenz gauge)
key_equations.meaning: Leading slow-motion radiation field; not yet in TT gauge. The book prints the exponent as -i Omega (r - t); the sign here matches Eq. 9.74.

key_equations.name: TT quadrupole field along z
key_equations.latex: \bar h^{\rm TT}_{zi}=0,\quad \bar h^{\rm TT}_{xx}=-\bar h^{\rm TT}_{yy}=-\Omega^2(\mathcal I_{xx}-\mathcal I_{yy})e^{i\Omega r}/r,\quad \bar h^{\rm TT}_{xy}=-2\Omega^2\mathcal I_{xy}e^{i\Omega r}/r
key_equations.meaning: Observable polarizations for radiation travelling along z, built from the reduced quadrupole; the e^{-i Omega t} factor is implicit in the book's printing.
key_equations.symbols: I (calligraphic): reduced quadrupole amplitude.

key_equations.name: Reduced quadrupole
key_equations.meaning: Trace-free part of the mass quadrupole; only it radiates.

key_equations.name: Quadrupole of a vibrating spring
key_equations.meaning: Two oscillating masses give components at omega and 2 omega.
key_equations.symbols: A: amplitude of each mass; l_0: mean separation.

key_equations.name: Radiation from the vibrating spring
key_equations.meaning: Linearly polarized, aligned with the spring, zero along the spring's axis (Eq. 9.91). Printed Eq. 9.92 shows A instead of A^2, and the middle line of Eq. 9.88 omits m.

key_equations.name: Equal-mass circular orbit
key_equations.meaning: Kepler's law for two masses m at separation l_0.

key_equations.name: Binary quadrupole
key_equations.meaning: Time-varying reduced quadrupole of a circular binary oscillates at twice the orbital frequency.

key_equations.name: Binary radiation along the orbital axis
key_equations.meaning: Circularly polarized radiation at frequency 2 omega perpendicular to the orbit.

key_equations.name: Binary radiation in the orbital plane
key_equations.meaning: Linearly polarized, half the plus amplitude seen face-on.

key_equations.name: Binary radiation at inclination iota
key_equations.meaning: Interpolates between circular (face-on) and linear (edge-on) polarization; still to be TT-projected along the line of sight.
key_equations.symbols: iota: inclination of orbital normal to the line of sight.

key_equations.name: Amplitude estimate
key_equations.meaning: For a self-gravitating source, the wave amplitude is at most the product of the internal potential and the source's potential at the observer.
