key_equations.symbols: phi_0: typical internal Newtonian potential; phi_r = M/r.

key_equations.name: Retarded integral
key_equations.meaning: Exact outgoing solution of Eq. 9.64 for any source.

key_equations.name: Far-field limit of retarded integral
key_equations.meaning: Replace R by r for a distant field point and slowly varying source.

key_equations.name: General quadrupole field and TT form
key_equations.latex: \bar h_{jk}(t,x^i)=\frac2r\ddot I_{jk}(t-r),\qquad \bar h^{\rm TT}_{xx}=\frac1r\left[\ddot{\mathcal I}_{xx}(t-r)-\ddot{\mathcal I}_{yy}(t-r)\right],\quad \bar h^{\rm TT}_{xy}=\frac2r\ddot{\mathcal I}_{xy}(t-r)
key_equations.meaning: Arbitrary time dependence; the field is the second time derivative of the quadrupole at retarded time. Printed with a leading minus sign in 9.106 and with the second line of 9.107 labelled h_xx; both are corrected here for consistency with Eq. 9.83.
key_equations.symbols: dots: time derivatives.

key_equations.name: Power absorbed by one oscillator
key_equations.meaning: Frictional loss balanced by work done by the wave's tidal force in steady state.

key_equations.name: Flux loss through a plane of oscillators
key_equations.meaning: Energy per area per time removed from the wave.
key_equations.symbols: sigma: oscillators per unit area.

key_equations.name: Field radiated by one driven oscillator
key_equations.meaning: Quadrupole of the oscillator with mass amplitude R/2; its 2 Omega term is negligible.

key_equations.name: Summed field of the oscillator plane
key_equations.meaning: Using varpi d varpi = r dr and a convergence factor exp(-epsilon r), the plane emits a net plane wave.
key_equations.symbols: varpi: radius in the plane from the foot point Q.

key_equations.name: Net downstream wave
key_equations.latex: \delta\bar h^{\rm TT}_{xx}=2\pi\sigma m\Omega l_0R\sin[\Omega(z-t)-\phi],\quad \bar h^{\rm net}_{xx}=(A-2\pi\sigma m\Omega l_0R\sin\phi)\cos[\Omega(z-t)-\psi],\quad \tan\psi=\frac{2\pi\sigma m\Omega l_0R}{A}\cos\phi
key_equations.meaning: After TT projection and superposition the incident amplitude is reduced and slightly phase-shifted.
key_equations.symbols: psi: small phase shift.

key_equations.name: Amplitude reduction and flux-amplitude relation
key_equations.meaning: Dividing the flux loss by the amplitude loss, all oscillator parameters cancel.

key_equations.name: Energy flux of a monochromatic wave
key_equations.meaning: Flux of a linearly polarized plane wave of amplitude A (geometrized units).

key_equations.name: Flux in TT invariant form
key_equations.meaning: Applies to any polarization and any small patch of wavefront; background-Lorentz invariant but not gauge invariant.

key_equations.name: Flux on the z axis from a quadrupole source
key_equations.latex: F=\frac{\Omega^6}{32\pi r^2}\langle2(\mathcal I_{xx}-\mathcal I_{yy})^2+8\mathcal I_{xy}^2\rangle=\frac{\Omega^6}{16\pi r^2}\langle2\mathcal I_{ij}\mathcal I^{ij}-4\mathcal I_{zj}\mathcal I_z{}^j+\mathcal I_{zz}^2\rangle
key_equations.meaning: Rewritten with the trace-free identity so the special direction appears explicitly. The first form is printed as 8 I^{xy} without the square; corrected here.

key_equations.name: Flux in direction n
key_equations.latex: F=\frac{\Omega^6}{16\pi r^2}\langle2\mathcal I_{ij}\mathcal I^{ij}-4n^jn^k\mathcal I_{ji}\mathcal I_k{}^i+n^in^jn^kn^l\mathcal I_{ij}\mathcal I_{kl}\rangle
key_equations.meaning: Angular pattern of the radiated flux.
key_equations.symbols: n^j = x^j/r.

key_equations.name: Angular integrals
key_equations.meaning: Symmetry fixes the tensor form; one component fixes the constant.
key_equations.symbols: d Omega = sin theta d theta d phi.

key_equations.name: Quadrupole luminosity (sinusoidal)
key_equations.meaning: Total power radiated by a slow periodic source.

key_equations.name: Quadrupole luminosity (general)
key_equations.meaning: Power radiated in terms of the third time derivative of the reduced quadrupole.

key_equations.name: Luminosity bound
key_equations.meaning: Luminosity scales as phi_0^2 v^6 and cannot exceed about c^5/G.

key_equations.name: Equal-mass circular binary luminosity
key_equations.meaning: Luminosity depends steeply on orbital frequency.
key_equations.symbols: M: mass of each star; omega: orbital angular velocity.

key_equations.name: Luminosity conversion
key_equations.latex: L_{\rm SI}=\frac{c^5}{G}L_{\rm geom}=3.63\times10^{52}\ {\rm J\,s^{-1}}\times L_{\rm geom}
key_equations.meaning: Convert dimensionless geometrized luminosity to watts.

key_equations.name: Newtonian energy of the binary
key_equations.meaning: Binding energy of the equal-mass circular orbit; -1.11e-3 m for Hulse-Taylor numbers.
key_equations.symbols: r = l_0/2: orbital radius.

key_equations.name: Period decay estimate
key_equations.meaning: Circular-orbit prediction for PSR B1913+16, about -6 microseconds per year.

key_equations.name: Hulse-Taylor prediction and observation
key_equations.meaning: Eccentric-orbit GR prediction agrees with timing to 0.17 percent. Printed Eq. 9.147 gives -7.2e-15 s/yr; the correct conversion is about -7.6e-5 s/yr.

key_equations.name: Unequal-mass binary amplitudes
key_equations.latex: \bar h_{xx}=-\bar h_{yy}=-4\mu M^{2/3}\omega^{2/3}e^{2i\omega(r-t)}/r,\quad \bar h_{xy}=-4i\mu M^{2/3}\omega^{2/3}e^{2i\omega(r-t)}/r;\quad \bar h^{\rm TT}_{yy}=-\bar h^{\rm TT}_{zz}=2\mu M^{2/3}\omega^{2/3}e^{2i\omega(r-t)}/r
key_equations.meaning: Face-on and edge-on amplitudes depend on masses only through mu M^{2/3}.
key_equations.symbols: M = m1 + m2; mu = m1 m2/M.

key_equations.name: Chirp mass
key_equations.meaning: The single mass scale of a circular binary's leading-order signal.

key_equations.name: Binary waveform in chirp-mass form
key_equations.latex: \bar h_{xx}=-\bar h_{yy}=-2\frac{\mathcal M}{r}(\mathcal M\omega)^{2/3}\left[1+\cos^2\iota\right]e^{2i(\mathcal M\omega)(r-t)/\mathcal M},\quad \bar h_{xy}=-4i\frac{\mathcal M}{r}(\mathcal M\omega)^{2/3}\cos\iota\,e^{2i(\mathcal M\omega)(r-t)/\mathcal M}
key_equations.meaning: Chirp mass is the only scale: doubling it while halving the frequency gives the same amplitude at double the distance.

key_equations.name: Luminosity and energy in chirp-mass form
key_equations.meaning: Both depend only on the dimensionless product of chirp mass and orbital frequency.
key_equations.symbols: omega: orbital, not gravitational-wave, angular frequency.

key_equations.name: Chirp mass from frequency evolution
key_equations.meaning: Measure omega and omega-dot at any moment to get the chirp mass.

key_equations.name: Chirp time and time to merger
key_equations.meaning: Characteristic and total remaining inspiral times; the latter is 3/8 of the former.

key_equations.name: Remaining phase and luminosity
key_equations.meaning: Luminosity is fixed by the number of orbits left, independent of mass.
key_equations.symbols: psi: orbital phase.

key_equations.name: Luminosity-flux-distance
key_equations.meaning: Inverse-square law for an isotropic source.

key_equations.name: Standard-siren distance
key_equations.meaning: Distance from measured amplitude, frequency and chirp mass; alpha collects orientation factors of order 1.
key_equations.symbols: h: amplitude measured in one detector.

key_equations.name: Redshifted chirp mass
key_equations.meaning: Detector-frame mass is larger by 1 + z; the inferred distance is a luminosity distance.
key_equations.symbols: z: redshift.

key_equations.name: TT projection operator form
key_equations.meaning: Transverse-traceless part of a radiation field travelling along n (Exercise 9.33).

key_equations.name: Frequency drift
key_equations.meaning: Energy balance for a circular binary (Exercise 9.41).

key_equations.name: Isaacson stress-energy tensor
key_equations.meaning: Averaged effective stress-energy of waves; T^{0z} reproduces Eq. 9.123 (Exercise 9.50).

key_equations.name: Peters-Mathews energy loss
key_equations.meaning: Orbit-averaged power of an eccentric binary; the enhancement factor is about 12 for e = 0.617 (Exercise 9.56).
key_equations.symbols: a: semi-major axis; e: eccentricity; m, M: the two masses.

key_equations.name: Orbital element decay rates
key_equations.meaning: Peters (1964) formulas; eccentricity decays faster than the orbit shrinks.

figures.label: Figure 9.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A ring of free test particles before a wave moving along z arrives (a), and its distortion at two phases half a cycle apart for plus polarization (b) and cross polarization (c); positions reflect proper distances.
figures.visual_description: Three side-by-side boxed panels. Panel (a): eight black dots evenly spaced on a circle around a central dot, with small x (right) and y (up) axis arrows below. Panel (b): two stacked ellipses of dots around a central dot; the upper one, labelled t = t1, is elongated vertically with outward arrows at top and bottom and inward arrows at left and right; the lower one, labelled t = t2, is elongated horizontally with outward arrows at left and right and inward arrows at top and bottom. Panel (c): the same pair of ellipses but tilted by 45 degrees, the upper (t = t1) stretched along one diagonal and the lower (t = t2) along the other, with inward arrows along the short diagonal.
figures.what_it_teaches: The two independent polarizations act as area-preserving quadrupolar squeezes transverse to the propagation direction, alternating each half period, and the cross pattern is the plus pattern rotated by 45 degrees; it also shows where to place interferometer arms.

redesign.idea: Live ring of test particles (optionally a 3D lattice of rings along z) driven by a user-defined wave with independent plus and cross amplitudes and a relative phase, with ghost interferometer arms overlaid.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for h_+, h_x, relative phase (0 gives linear, 90 degrees gives circular), frequency, and wave direction; toggles to show displacement vectors versus tidal acceleration vectors, and to rotate the arms; a readout of the arm-length difference signal updates in real time and goes to zero for a cross wave overhead with arms on x and y.

figures.label: Figure 9.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Idealized bar detector: two equal masses joined by a spring.
figures.visual_description: Two grey filled circles, each labelled m underneath, at left and right ends of a horizontal coiled spring drawn as a long helix. Labels x1(t) above the left mass and x2(t) above the right mass indicate their time-dependent positions.
figures.what_it_teaches: The minimal material model for how a wave's tidal force drives a bound system; the same device is reused as a radiator and as the energy-flux calibrator.
concepts: tidal force of a gravitational wave

redesign.idea: Animated two-mass spring driven by an incoming sinusoidal wave, with exaggerated strain, coupled to a resonance-curve plot and a thermal-noise band.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for wave frequency, natural frequency, Q, mass, length and temperature; the plot of response amplitude versus frequency and the time trace of stretch update, with a k_B T noise floor showing when the signal is buried; a button to switch to Weber-bar numbers.

figures.label: Figure 9.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Optical layout of a Fabry-Perot interferometer like LIGO or Virgo: laser, power-recycling mirror, beamsplitter, near and far mirrors forming arm cavities, photodetector at the dark port, all optics suspended.
figures.visual_description: Perspective line drawing. A laser (grey box, upper left) sends a beam to the right through a disc labelled power recycling mirror to a small tilted beamsplitter at the centre. From the beamsplitter a thick dark bar labelled Arm 1 runs toward the lower left, passing a near mirror and ending at a large disc labelled far mirror; another thick bar labelled Arm 2 runs to the right to a second far-mirror disc, passing its near mirror close to the beamsplitter. Double-headed arrows lie alongside both arms. A photodetector sits above and behind the beamsplitter with a dashed beam to it. Every mirror, the beamsplitter and the recycling mirror hang from hatched ceiling supports by thin V-shaped wires, indicating pendulum suspensions.
figures.what_it_teaches: How the abstract two-arm timing comparison is realized: cavities store light to enhance phase shifts, recycling reuses the bright-port light, the dark port carries the signal, and suspensions isolate the test masses.
concepts: Fabry-Perot arm cavities and power recycling

redesign.idea: Explorable 3D interferometer in which a passing wave changes arm lengths, cavity-stored photons build up, and the dark-port brightness responds; an adjacent strain-sensitivity curve shows seismic, thermal and shot-noise contributions.
redesign.interaction: Toggle cavities and recycling on or off to see the signal gain; drag the mirror reflectivity; set laser power to move the shot-noise curve; inject a chirp and watch the photodetector output and the noise-limited band change.

figures.label: Figure 9.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Aerial photograph of the LIGO Hanford site with one 4-km arm receding into the distance; caption gives coordinates of the world's detectors.
figures.visual_description: Black-and-white aerial photograph of flat, scrubby desert with low hills on the horizon. A thin straight light line (the vacuum-tube enclosure of one arm) runs diagonally from a cluster of buildings at lower right toward the upper left, with a small building midway along it. A second straight line runs from the buildings to the left edge of the frame along the bottom.
figures.what_it_teaches: The kilometre scale needed because the strain effect grows with baseline; the L-shaped geometry of a real detector.

redesign.idea: Rotatable globe with the listed detector sites and true arm orientations, used to demonstrate network localization and antenna response.
redesign.interaction: Place a source on the sky; the app computes arrival-time delays and draws the delay rings between detector pairs, their intersections, and each detector's response to plus and cross polarization; turn detectors on or off to see how the localization patch shrinks.

figures.label: Figure 9.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: A detector excited by an incident wave re-radiates, and downstream the re-radiated and incident waves interfere destructively.
figures.visual_description: A vertical coil spring with a black dot at each end sits in the middle. Three solid horizontal arrows on the left, labelled Incident wave and Upstream, point at it. Four dashed arrows radiate diagonally outward from the two masses, labelled Radiated wave at the top. On the right, three solid arrows alternate with two shorter dashed arrows all pointing right, labelled Destructive interference and Downstream.
figures.what_it_teaches: Energy absorbed by a detector must be paid for by a weaker transmitted wave, and the mechanism is interference between incident and scattered radiation.
concepts: energy flux of a gravitational wave

redesign.idea: Animated wavefield showing an incident plane wave, the oscillator's re-radiated quadrupolar wave, and their sum, with an energy ledger comparing power absorbed with the drop in downstream flux.
redesign.interaction: Adjust oscillator damping and detuning; watch the phase lag phi, the downstream amplitude deficit and the absorbed power change together, confirming their ratio stays Omega^2 A/(16 pi).

figures.label: Figure 9.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Many detectors spread over the plane z = 0 with areal density sigma, facing an incident wave.
figures.visual_description: A parallelogram drawn in perspective to represent a plane, filled with a regular grid of small black dots. Three horizontal arrows on the left, labelled Incident wave, point toward the plane. A label at upper right reads sigma oscillators per unit area.
figures.what_it_teaches: Converting single-oscillator absorption into a flux (per unit area) statement, and setting up a Huygens-like sum that yields a plane wave.
concepts: energy flux of a gravitational wave

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.2: plane-wave solution of the vacuum equations
worked_examples.problem: Find conditions under which a complex plane wave solves the vacuum linearized equations in Lorenz gauge.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate the exponential to replace derivatives by i k, reduce the wave equation to an algebraic condition, then apply the gauge condition to the amplitude; interpret constant-phase surfaces using a photon world line.
worked_examples.key_insight: Derivatives on a plane wave are algebraic, so nullity of k and transversality of A drop out immediately.
worked_examples.result: k must be null (omega^2 = |k|^2) and A^{alpha beta} k_beta = 0.

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.2: reduction to TT gauge
worked_examples.problem: Use the remaining gauge freedom to simplify the plane-wave amplitude as far as possible.
worked_examples.method: Generate a gauge change with a plane-wave vector of the same k, write the amplitude shift, impose trace-free and U-orthogonality (details in Exercise 9.5), then go to U's rest frame with k along z and read off surviving components.
worked_examples.key_insight: Four gauge parameters remove exactly the non-physical components; what survives cannot be transformed away and is physical.

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.2: free particles and proper distance
worked_examples.problem: Determine how a passing wave affects free particles initially at rest.
worked_examples.method: Evaluate the geodesic equation's initial acceleration in TT gauge, find it zero, then integrate sqrt(g_xx) between two coordinate-fixed particles.
worked_examples.key_insight: Coordinate positions are fixed by the gauge choice; only the invariant proper distance reveals the wave.

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.2: geodesic deviation and Riemann components
worked_examples.problem: Describe the relative acceleration of nearby free particles in a gauge-invariant way.
worked_examples.method: Work in the local inertial frame of one particle so the covariant derivative becomes ordinary; keep U at zeroth order; evaluate R in TT gauge using gauge invariance; specialize to x- and y-separated pairs.
worked_examples.key_insight: Relative accelerations measure Riemann directly and match the proper-distance result, and the deviation form admits other forces.
concepts: geodesic deviation in a gravitational wave
gauge invariance of the linearized Riemann tensor
tidal force of a gravitational wave

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.2: exact nonlinear plane wave
worked_examples.problem: Find an exact vacuum solution resembling the linear plane wave.
worked_examples.method: Adopt null coordinates, guess a metric depending only on u with transverse scale factors, compute Christoffel symbols and Riemann, impose Ricci flatness, and linearize.
worked_examples.key_insight: The nonlinear theory admits the same freedom of an arbitrary waveform; the linear wave is its weak limit.
worked_examples.result: f''/f + g''/g = 0; for g = 1 + epsilon, f is approximately 1 - epsilon.

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.3: bar detector response equation
worked_examples.problem: Derive the equation of motion for the stretch of a two-mass spring hit by a wave along z.
worked_examples.method: (1) Newton's law in a local inertial frame at one mass equals TT form to first order; (2) spring force uses proper length l = (x2 - x1)(1 + h_xx^TT/2); (3) define xi = l - l_0, invert for x2 - x1, and subtract the two equations.
worked_examples.key_insight: The wave enters only through the proper-length correction, yet the result is the tidal forcing of Eq. 9.28a, a consistency check.
worked_examples.result: xi'' + 2 gamma xi' + omega_0^2 xi = l_0 h_xx,00^TT / 2 (Eq. 9.45).
concepts: tidal force of a gravitational wave

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.3: resonant response and Weber-bar numbers
worked_examples.problem: Find the steady response and energy of a bar driven on resonance, and evaluate for a Weber bar with A = 1e-20.
worked_examples.method: Solve the driven oscillator; time-average kinetic plus potential energy; set omega_0 = Omega; express in Q; insert m = 1.4e3 kg, l_0 = 1.5 m, omega_0 = 1e4 per second, Q = 1e5.
worked_examples.key_insight: Even an optimistic wave gives a nucleus-sized displacement and energy comparable with room-temperature thermal noise.
worked_examples.result: R about 1e-15 m, E about 1e-20 J (Eqs. 9.54-9.57).

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.3: radar round trip in a wave metric
worked_examples.problem: Compute the proper time for light to go from one free mass to another at coordinate distance L and back, and its rate of change.
worked_examples.method: Null condition gives coordinate speed; integrate dt = (1 + h_+)^{1/2} dx replacing t(x) in h_+ by its flat value; add the return leg; differentiate with respect to t_start so each integral of a derivative collapses to endpoint values.
worked_examples.key_insight: Differentiating the return time eliminates the integrals, so the response depends on the wave only at emission and reception (for perpendicular incidence).
concepts: return-time response of a beam detector

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.4: amplitude ceiling examples
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the largest plausible amplitude from a supernova forming a 10 solar mass black hole at 1e23 m, and from a pair of 30 solar mass black holes at 1e25 m.
worked_examples.method: Use h of order M/R, with masses converted to metres.
worked_examples.key_insight: Comparing the ceiling (1e-20) with the observed 1e-21 for GW150914 shows the metric near the merger was distorted by roughly 10 percent.

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.4: slow-motion quadrupole field
worked_examples.problem: Solve the sourced wave equation for a small, sinusoidally oscillating source.
worked_examples.method: Factor out e^{-i Omega t}; outside, take the outgoing 1/r solution; integrate the Helmholtz equation over a ball of radius epsilon with Gauss's theorem; drop the Omega^2 term; use conservation to kill J^{mu 0}; apply the tensor virial identity; TT-project.
worked_examples.key_insight: Indices are spectators until conservation laws are used; then energy-momentum conservation leaves the quadrupole as the leading radiator.
worked_examples.result: h-bar_jk = -2 Omega^2 D_jk e^{i Omega (r-t)}/r and TT components in terms of the reduced quadrupole (Eqs. 9.74-9.87).
concepts: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.4: radiation from a vibrating spring
worked_examples.problem: Find the waves from two masses oscillating along x about separation l_0 and estimate a laboratory generator.
worked_examples.method: Compute I_xx, split into omega and 2 omega parts, form the reduced quadrupole, evaluate Eqs. 9.85-9.86 along z and (after permuting axes) along x; insert m = 1e3 kg, l_0 = 1 m, A = 1e-4 m, omega = 1e4 per second.
worked_examples.key_insight: Radiation is linearly polarized along the spring and vanishes along its axis; laboratory sources are hopelessly weak.
worked_examples.result: h_xx^TT = -[2 m omega^2 l_0 A cos omega(r-t) + 4 m omega^2 A^2 cos 2 omega(r-t)]/r; book quotes about 1e-34/r (our arithmetic gives about 2e-37/r).

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.4: equal-mass circular binary
worked_examples.problem: Find the gravitational waves from two stars of mass m in a circular orbit of separation l_0.
worked_examples.method: Kepler's law for omega; positions give I_ij oscillating at 2 omega; complex reduced quadrupole with a factor i in I_xy; evaluate along the orbital axis and in the plane; quote the general inclination form.
worked_examples.key_insight: The i in I_xy means the two polarizations are a quarter cycle apart face-on (circular), while edge-on only one survives (linear).
worked_examples.result: Amplitude 2 m l_0^2 omega^2/r at frequency 2 omega, of order (m omega)^{2/3} m/r (Eqs. 9.98-9.100); about 1e-20 quoted for PSR B1913+16.

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.4: wave force versus Newtonian tidal force
worked_examples.problem: Explain why a distant source's waves can be detectable although its static gravity is not.
worked_examples.method: Compare the wave tidal acceleration h l_0 omega^2 with the Newtonian tidal acceleration phi_r l_0/r^2, using h ~ phi_0 phi_r and omega ~ v/R.
worked_examples.key_insight: Waves fall off as 1/r while tides fall as 1/r^3, so the ratio grows as (phi_0 r/R)^2; this also marks where a Newtonian description of the field breaks down (r ~ R/phi_0).
worked_examples.result: Factor about 1e22 for phi_0 = 0.1, R = 1e11 m, r = 1e23 m.
concepts: tidal force of a gravitational wave

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.5: energy flux from a sheet of oscillators
worked_examples.problem: Determine the energy flux carried by a plane gravitational wave without field-theoretic energy definitions.
worked_examples.method: Compute average power absorbed per oscillator; sum the quadrupole fields of a plane of oscillators with density sigma using a convergence factor; TT-project; superpose with the incident wave to find the amplitude reduction; divide flux change by amplitude change using the steady-state R and phi; integrate in A.
worked_examples.key_insight: Assuming only energy conservation, all detector parameters cancel, leaving a property of the wave itself.
worked_examples.result: F = Omega^2 A^2/(32 pi) = Omega^2 <h^TT h^TT>/(32 pi) (Eqs. 9.121-9.123).
concepts: energy flux of a gravitational wave

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.5: total luminosity of a quadrupole source
worked_examples.problem: Integrate the flux of a general slow-motion source over a sphere.
worked_examples.method: Write F on the z axis in terms of the reduced quadrupole, use trace-freeness to isolate z-dependence, replace z by n^j, integrate using symmetric angular tensor identities.
worked_examples.key_insight: Symmetry alone fixes the angular integrals, so the total power reduces to a single contraction of the quadrupole.
worked_examples.result: L = (1/5) Omega^6 <I_ij I^ij>, generally (1/5) <dddot I_ij dddot I^ij> (Eqs. 9.131-9.133).

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.5: maximum luminosity argument
worked_examples.problem: Show that no source can have luminosity much above c^5/G.
worked_examples.method: Radiation flux L/R^2 through a region of size R implies energy density at least of that order and total radiation energy at least LR; its Newtonian potential is at least L; potentials above 1 mean a black hole.
worked_examples.key_insight: The bound applies to all radiation, not just gravitational, and is a pure consequence of units and horizon formation.
worked_examples.result: L of order 1 = c^5/G, about 3.6e52 W.

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.5: Hulse-Taylor period decay
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the rate of change of the Hulse-Taylor binary period assuming a circular orbit.
worked_examples.method: Luminosity from the quadrupole formula (8/5) M^2 l_0^4 omega^6 with l_0 eliminated; Newtonian energy -M^2/(4r); log-differentiate E(omega); set dE/dt = -L; evaluate in metres.
worked_examples.key_insight: Working in geometrized units makes dP/dt manifestly dimensionless; eccentricity raises the loss about twelvefold via the omega^6 dependence near periastron.
worked_examples.result: L = 1.71e-29, E = -1.11e-3 m, dP/dt about -2.0e-13 (circular) versus -2.40e-12 with eccentricity and observed -(2.398 +/- 0.004)e-12.

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.6: chirp-mass scaling relations
worked_examples.problem: Express the waveform, energy, and evolution of an unequal-mass circular binary in terms of observables.
worked_examples.method: Replace m by 2 mu and l_0 by (M/omega^2)^{1/3}; identify the chirp mass; energy balance dE/dt = -L gives omega-dot; form chirp time; integrate dt/d omega and d psi/d omega to infinity; eliminate (M omega) between L and psi.
worked_examples.key_insight: Every dimensionless observable depends only on the chirp mass times the orbital frequency, so the signal is self-calibrating.
worked_examples.result: M_chirp = (5/96)^{3/5} omega-dot^{3/5} omega^{-11/5}; tau_merger = (3/8) tau_chirp; L = 1/(160 psi^2) (Eqs. 9.153-9.160).
concepts: remaining orbital phase and mass-independent luminosity

worked_examples.label: In-text calculation §9.6: distance to a standard siren
worked_examples.problem: Infer the distance of an inspiralling binary from its gravitational-wave signal.
worked_examples.method: From omega and omega-dot get the chirp mass; from network polarization get inclination; amplitude formula (9.152) inverted gives r; include redshift so masses become (1+z) times source values and r a luminosity distance.
worked_examples.key_insight: Gravity supplies the intrinsic luminosity through the chirp, the way a known bulb wattage calibrates a standard candle.
worked_examples.result: r = alpha M_chirp (M_chirp omega)^{2/3}/h with M_obs = (1+z) M_true (Eqs. 9.162-9.163).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Gravitational-wave detectors as microphones; the waves as cosmic sound
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Both record the phase of long-wavelength waves, cannot focus on a direction, locate sources with arrays and phase delays, and receive coherent emission from bulk motions; hence the vocabulary of listening, chirps and sirens.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Sound needs a medium and travels slowly; gravitational waves are transverse quadrupolar strains moving at c, and detectors respond to strain, not pressure.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Play a detected-style chirp as audio while a spectrogram and a microphone-array analogy show how delays between sites localize a sound source and a gravitational-wave source alike.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Standard candle (known luminosity) becomes a standard siren
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Just as astronomers get distance from a source of known brightness, the chirp of a binary reveals its intrinsic gravitational luminosity, so its amplitude gives distance.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Unlike candles, sirens need no empirical calibration ladder, but they require polarization or sky information to remove inclination and they measure luminosity distance with redshift degeneracy.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Slider app: match a light bulb's apparent brightness to distance, then do the same with a chirp whose sweep rate sets the loudness.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Charge conservation forbids electromagnetic monopole radiation; energy-momentum conservation forbids gravitational monopole and dipole radiation
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: absence of monopole and dipole gravitational radiation
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why the leading gravitational radiation is quadrupolar and why spherically symmetric motion does not radiate.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Electromagnetism does allow dipole radiation, because charges of both signs can separate; gravity's dipole is the centre of mass, fixed by momentum conservation.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Multipole ladder: animate a pulsating sphere, a sloshing dipole and a rotating dumbbell side by side for electric charge and for mass, showing which radiate.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Electromagnetic polarizations separated by 90 degrees versus gravitational polarizations by 45 degrees
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Contrasts a vector field (spin-1) with a symmetric tensor field (spin-2) through how far a pattern must rotate to look like the other independent state.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The rotation angle argument does not by itself establish quantum spin; the book only gestures at the rank of the field.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Rotate a ring of test charges under an EM wave and a ring of test masses under a GW wave; show the angle at which each pattern first maps into its orthogonal partner.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Timing a reflected light pulse is the familiar way to measure distance and, because of light's privileged role, measures proper distance in curved spacetime too.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Valid as proper distance only when the separation is small compared with the gravitational wavelength; otherwise the return time mixes wave values at different times.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: One interferometer arm serves as the clock for the other
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why interferometers beat single-beam detectors: comparing two return times removes the need for an ultra-stable atomic clock.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The comparison only works if the arms respond differently to the wave; a cross wave overhead with arms on x and y gives no signal.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Race two photons down perpendicular arms while a wave passes; show their arrival-time difference with and without a noisy shared clock.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Pendulum suspensions as mechanical low-pass filters; active isolation like noise-cancelling headphones
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Makes the engineering of vibration isolation intuitive.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Real suspensions have internal modes and thermal noise; active control has its own sensor noise.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Shake the top of a single and a triple pendulum at variable frequency and plot transmitted motion versus frequency.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Folding the light path many times
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: Fabry-Perot arm cavities and power recycling
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Arm cavities are presented as the equivalent of bouncing the beam up and down the arm repeatedly to lengthen its storage time.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A cavity is a resonant device with finite bandwidth; storage times longer than the wave period reduce high-frequency response.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Names the rising-frequency signal of an inspiralling binary.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Gravity has only one sign of charge, so emitters add coherently, like pressure changes producing sound
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why gravitational radiation comes from bulk motions rather than individual atomic transitions, unlike light from incoherently emitting atoms.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Microscopic gravitational emission exists in principle but is utterly negligible; the point is about which contribution dominates.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Waves in curved spacetime behave like electromagnetic waves in a complicated medium
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Short waves follow null geodesics, transport polarization, and can be lensed, just like light.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Unlike light, gravitational waves are almost unaffected by matter along their path.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Underwater acoustic arrays for geophysics and defence
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Direction to a source is found from phase or time delays across widely separated sensors.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Gravitational-wave networks have very few sensors and strongly direction-dependent antenna patterns.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because free particles keep constant coordinates in TT gauge, a gravitational wave has no effect on them.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Constant TT coordinates just mean the coordinates are attached to free particles; the proper distance between particles changes, which is measurable.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: A coordinate calculation seems to show the particle is 'at rest', and at-rest language suggests nothing happens.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If a wave stretches space, rulers stretch too, so the stretching can never be measured.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Rulers are held together by electromagnetic forces far stronger than the wave's tidal force, so they barely change length; free masses do move relative to them. Light-travel timing is an even better measure.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: A ruler is mostly empty space, and 'space stretching' sounds like everything inside it expands uniformly.
concepts: stretching of space and rigid rulers
tidal force of a gravitational wave

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An interferometer compares arm lengths with the laser wavelength, and since the wave also stretches the light, the effect cancels.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The interferometer compares round-trip times of light on null paths; what happens to the wavelength along the way is irrelevant, and wavelength is observer-dependent anyway (footnote 2).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Textbook pictures of interference count wavelengths, so it seems the ruler is the wavelength.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The coordinate speed of light (1 + h_+)^{-1/2} being different from 1 violates relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only locally measured speeds must equal 1; coordinate speeds in arbitrary coordinates can differ, and the measurable return time is computed with proper time.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Special relativity is often summarized as 'light always moves at c' without the 'locally, in an inertial frame' qualifier.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational waves might be mere wiggles of the coordinates rather than of geometry.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Riemann tensor, which is gauge invariant, is nonzero and directly sets measurable relative accelerations; waves also deposit energy in detectors and drain energy from binaries.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Einstein himself worried about this, and in linearized theory gauge changes do produce wave-like metric perturbations with no curvature (Exercise 9.10).
concepts: gauge invariance of the linearized Riemann tensor
geodesic deviation in a gravitational wave

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The two polarizations of gravitational waves are perpendicular to each other like those of light.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are rotated by 45 degrees relative to each other, reflecting the rank-2 tensor nature of the field.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Light is the familiar model of polarization.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An interferometer is sensitive to every wave that passes through it.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It responds to one linear combination of polarizations; a cross-polarized wave arriving perpendicular to both arms aligned with the plus axes produces no signal, and response varies with direction.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Interferometers are described as nearly omnidirectional.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A spherically symmetric supernova collapse should be a strong gravitational-wave source because it involves huge masses moving fast.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Spherically symmetric motion does not radiate at all; only the non-spherical part of the motion contributes, so realistic amplitudes can be far below the h ~ phi_0 phi_r estimate.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Energy and speed seem to be what matters, as for explosions in general.
concepts: no gravitational radiation from spherically symmetric motion

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If the leading-order quadrupole moment does not change, the system emits no gravitational waves.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The quadrupole formula gives only the dominant term; a rotating square of equal masses has a constant quadrupole but radiates through higher multipoles.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The formula is used so often that it is taken as exact.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since the wave amplitude is no larger than the Newtonian potential of the source at Earth, it should be even harder to detect than the source's static gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: What detectors sense is force; the wave tidal force h l omega^2 falls as 1/r and exceeds the static tidal force (falling as 1/r^3) by a factor (phi_0 r/R)^2, enormous at astronomical distances.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Comparing dimensionless amplitudes seems the natural test of detectability.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational-wave energy can be localized at each point like electromagnetic energy density, in any gauge and at any order.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The flux formula is valid only as an average, only to lowest order in linearized theory, and is not gauge invariant; local gravitational energy has no general meaning in GR.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Electromagnetic energy density is local and gauge invariant, inviting the same expectation.
concepts: energy flux of a gravitational wave

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: In binary formulas, omega is the gravitational-wave frequency.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: omega is the orbital angular frequency; the dominant gravitational-wave angular frequency is twice it.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Radiation formulas usually use the frequency of the emitted wave.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Heavier merging black holes reach a higher peak gravitational luminosity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Peak luminosity depends only on the number of orbits remaining and is essentially the same (about 0.01 in geometrized units) for any mass; heavier systems radiate longer and so emit more total energy in proportion to their mass.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Bigger usually means brighter in astronomy.
concepts: remaining orbital phase and mass-independent luminosity

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A strain of 1e-21 means mirrors move by 1e-21 metres.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Strain is fractional; the length change is about h L/2 per arm (h L as an arm-length difference for a plus wave overhead), about 1e-18 m for 4-km arms.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Strain and displacement are easily conflated when numbers are quoted without units.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational-wave observations measure a binary's true masses directly.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Detectors measure only time-scales, so masses are redshifted by (1 + z) and must be corrected using the distance and a cosmological model.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Masses seem intrinsic and unaffected by motion.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The chirp mass is an intrinsically relativistic quantity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It already appears in the Newtonian orbital energy; it simply went unnoticed until gravitational-wave dynamics made it the controlling parameter.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It was introduced in a gravitational-wave context.

thought_experiments.name: Feynman's sticky beads
thought_experiments.setup: Two beads slide on a rod with friction while a gravitational wave passes; the tidal force moves them relative to the rod and friction heats it.
thought_experiments.lesson: Heat must be paid for by the wave, so gravitational waves carry energy; demanding conservation fixes the flux.
concepts: energy flux of a gravitational wave
thought_experiments.app_idea: Beads on a rod under an animated wave with a thermometer rising; toggling friction off leaves the beads oscillating with no heat.

thought_experiments.name: Ring of free particles
thought_experiments.setup: A circle of freely falling particles around a central one, initially at rest in a plane transverse to an incoming wave.
thought_experiments.lesson: The wave shears the ring into oscillating ellipses whose orientation distinguishes the two polarizations.

thought_experiments.name: A ruler in a gravitational wave
thought_experiments.setup: A solid ruler lies between two free particles while a wave passes.
thought_experiments.lesson: Internal forces dominate the tidal force, so the ruler keeps its length and can record the free particles' displacement.
concepts: stretching of space and rigid rulers
tidal force of a gravitational wave
thought_experiments.app_idea: Tune a 'stiffness' slider from zero (ruler follows free particles) to realistic (ruler rigid) while comparing lengths.

thought_experiments.name: A plane of absorbing oscillators
thought_experiments.setup: An infinite sheet of damped spring detectors, sigma per unit area, intercepts a plane wave.
thought_experiments.lesson: The re-radiated field forms a plane wave that reduces the downstream amplitude by exactly the absorbed energy, and the oscillators drop out of the flux formula.
concepts: energy flux of a gravitational wave

thought_experiments.name: Radar between two free masses
thought_experiments.setup: An observer at the centre of the particle ring sends photons to particles on the x and y axes and times their return.
thought_experiments.lesson: Return times differ by 2 h_+ L, a gauge-independent measurable that is the principle of interferometers (Exercise 9.26).

thought_experiments.name: Does a freely falling bowl of soup slosh?
thought_experiments.setup: A small bowl of soup, much smaller than a wavelength, falls freely as a wave passes (Exercise 9.8).
thought_experiments.lesson: Invites distinguishing the absence of acceleration at the centre of mass from tidal forces across the bowl.
concepts: tidal force of a gravitational wave

thought_experiments.name: Rotating square of equal masses
thought_experiments.setup: Four equal masses at the corners of a square spin about its centre (Exercise 9.31).
thought_experiments.lesson: The quadrupole moment stays constant, so the quadrupole formula predicts no radiation, yet higher multipoles radiate: leading-order formulas are not proofs.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Rotating mass configurations with a live readout of I_ij and the octupole moment.

thought_experiments.name: Rescaled binaries
thought_experiments.setup: Compare a binary with a given chirp mass and orbital frequency to one with twice the chirp mass and half the frequency, placed twice as far away.
thought_experiments.lesson: They produce identical amplitudes and phases once time is doubled: gravity has no intrinsic scale.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Overlay two chirps with a time-stretch slider that makes them coincide.

historical_notes.event: Derived the linearized description of gravitational waves, judged them far too weak to detect, and later doubted they were real rather than coordinate effects.
historical_notes.significance: Sets up the chapter's emphasis on invariant, measurable effects.

historical_notes.event: Found the solution now identified with black holes; Einstein did not accept it as describing real objects.
historical_notes.significance: Part of the framing that GR's astrophysical role was long underestimated.

historical_notes.event: Discovered the binary pulsar PSR B1913+16 in 1974, whose orbital decay provided evidence for gravitational radiation; Nobel Prize 1993.
historical_notes.significance: First strong, indirect confirmation that waves carry energy.

historical_notes.event: LIGO made the first direct detection on 14 September 2015 (a merger of two unexpectedly massive black holes); Nobel Prize 2017.
historical_notes.significance: Turned gravitational-wave physics into observational astronomy.

historical_notes.event: At the Chapel Hill conference Feynman gave the sticky-bead argument that waves carry energy; Bondi and Pirani made similar points; Weber was inspired to start detector work.
historical_notes.significance: Helped end decades of confusion about the reality and energy of waves, and provides the logic of §9.5.

historical_notes.event: Built the first resonant bar detectors and claimed detections in the late 1960s that other bars did not confirm.
historical_notes.significance: The controversy clouded the field, but the teams that tested his claims seeded later bar and interferometer projects.

historical_notes.event: Interferometers first reached sensitivity to relative length changes near 1e-21, approaching 1e-22 by 2015.
historical_notes.significance: Marks the technical milestone preceding detection.

historical_notes.event: Virgo joined LIGO in August 2017 and the network observed the first binary neutron star merger on 17 August 2017.
historical_notes.significance: Opened multimessenger gravitational-wave astronomy and standard-siren cosmology.

historical_notes.event: Derived that a binary's gravitational luminosity depends only on the number of orbits left, and other scaling results, before pulsars were known.
historical_notes.significance: An early, overlooked source of the standard-siren idea.

historical_notes.event: Wrote down the distance formula for binary standard sirens and pointed out their use for measuring the Hubble constant; with Krolak (1987) discussed cosmological redshift of observed masses.
historical_notes.significance: Foundation of gravitational-wave distance measurement used by LIGO-Virgo.

historical_notes.event: Computed radiation and orbital decay for eccentric binaries.
historical_notes.significance: Basis of the eccentricity correction for the Hulse-Taylor pulsar and of circularization arguments.

historical_notes.event: ESA's LISA Pathfinder, launched at the end of 2015, demonstrated drag-free free-fall performance better than LISA requires.
historical_notes.significance: Retired a key technical risk for space interferometry.

applications_and_observations.topic: Weber-type resonant bar excited by a strong continuous wave
applications_and_observations.details: Aluminium bar numbers inserted into the resonant response formulas show the displacement and deposited energy for an optimistic wave amplitude.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: m = 1.4e3 kg, l_0 = 1.5 m, omega_0 = 1e4 s^-1, Q about 1e5, A = 1e-20: E about 1e-20 J, R about 1e-15 m (nuclear size).

applications_and_observations.details: k_B T at room temperature is comparable to the signal energy; detecting a ten times weaker wave needs a hundred times lower temperature, so bars moved to about 3 K, and Auriga went below 100 mK.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: k_B = 1.38e-23 J/K; T about 300 K to 3 K to below 0.1 K.

applications_and_observations.details: The book justifies detection by analogy with the post-1960 opening of the electromagnetic spectrum, then names information only waves can carry: they leave supernova cores directly while light is scattered for days; detectable primordial waves may originate about 1e-25 s after the Big Bang; and the roughly 96 percent of mass-energy that does not interact electromagnetically still couples to gravity and might radiate.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Primordial waves from about 1e-25 s; ordinary matter about 4 percent of the Universe's mass-energy (as of writing; modern value about 5 percent).

applications_and_observations.topic: Bar readout, bandwidth and design limits
applications_and_observations.details: Weber's bar carried strain sensors at its waist where stretching is largest; later groups coupled the mode to a light resonant transducer to amplify motion and read it with superconducting SQUID electronics. Bars could not be made much longer (about 3 m at most) without isolation problems, Q was pushed with single sapphire crystals and spherical designs were proposed, but resonances above about 600 Hz sat above where most strong signals lie, and the needed 1e-21 burst sensitivity would have required beating the one-phonon quantum limit.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Bar lengths up to about 3 m; resonances above about 600 Hz; target burst amplitude about 1e-21.

applications_and_observations.details: Ground interferometers and bars above 1 Hz; LISA millihertz; decihertz gap for intermediate-mass black holes (DECIGO proposal); spacecraft tracking below 0.1 mHz; pulsar timing below 100 nHz; CMB polarization for primordial waves at about 1e-16 Hz today.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Ground band about 10 Hz-few kHz (advanced detectors 20 Hz-2 kHz); LISA above about 300 microhertz; LISA masses 1e4-1e7 solar; ground up to about 100 solar masses.

applications_and_observations.details: Radio transponders on interplanetary probes act as single-arm beam detectors; plasma delays and clock instability limit sensitivity; the three-term signature helps reject noise.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Round-trip times of hours; clock stability not yet 1e-19, so amplitudes of 1e-20 or less are out of reach.

applications_and_observations.details: Correlated timing residuals of many millisecond pulsars search for nanohertz waves; SKA would monitor hundreds of pulsars; the International Pulsar Timing Array coordinates efforts.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Sensitive below about 100 nHz; averages over months.

applications_and_observations.topic: Polarization of the cosmic microwave background
applications_and_observations.details: Primordial gravitational waves present at recombination imprint a polarization pattern; measuring it would probe early-Universe physics; details deferred to Chapter 13.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Wave frequency today about 1e-16 Hz.

applications_and_observations.topic: LIGO, Virgo, GEO600, KAGRA and LIGO-India
applications_and_observations.details: Kilometre-scale Fabry-Perot Michelson interferometers with suspended optics; GEO600 pioneered fused-silica monolithic suspensions; KAGRA is underground and cryogenic; LIGO-India is under construction.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: LIGO arms 4 km, 1.6 m diameter vacuum tubes, sites about 3000 km apart; Virgo 3 km; KAGRA 3 km with mirrors to 20 K; GEO600 600 m; suspension Q about 2e9; shot noise dominates above about 200 Hz.

applications_and_observations.details: LIGO detected a binary black hole merger on 14 September 2015 and further events over two years; with Virgo it observed the first binary neutron star merger on 17 August 2017.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Observed peak amplitude about 1e-21 for the first event.

applications_and_observations.details: h of order M/R gives ceilings for a nearby-galaxy supernova forming a black hole and for the first detected merger, implying order-10-percent metric distortion near the merging holes.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 10 solar masses at 1e23 m: 1e-17; 30 solar mass pair at 1e25 m: 1e-20 (observed 1e-21).

applications_and_observations.details: A tonne-scale vibrating spring produces an utterly negligible wave.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: m = 1e3 kg, l_0 = 1 m, A = 1e-4 m, omega = 1e4 s^-1: book quotes h about 1e-34/r (r in metres); our own evaluation of 2 m omega^2 l_0 A/r gives about 2e-37/r.

applications_and_observations.topic: Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar as a wave source and clock
applications_and_observations.details: Two 1.4 solar mass neutron stars in a 7 h 45 min orbit emit at twice the orbital frequency, below all planned detector bands; orbital decay tests the quadrupole formula.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: P = 27907 s = 8.3721e12 m; masses 2.07 km each; e = 0.617; GW frequency 72 microhertz; book states 8 kpc and amplitude 1e-20. Our check: the 1e-20 follows from the mis-printed 2.4e17 m; at the true 2.5e20 m the face-on amplitude is about 4e-23.

applications_and_observations.topic: Measured orbital decay of PSR B1913+16
applications_and_observations.details: Circular-orbit estimate followed by the eccentric-orbit GR prediction compared with timing data.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Circular estimate dP/dt = -2.0e-13 (-6e-6 s/yr); GR prediction -2.40263e-12; observed -(2.398 +/- 0.004)e-12; agreement 0.17 percent.

applications_and_observations.topic: Wave force versus Newtonian tidal force at astronomical distances
applications_and_observations.details: Illustrates why waves are detectable far beyond where the source's static tide could be felt.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: phi_0 = 0.1, R = 1e11 m, r = 1e23 m: ratio about 1e22.

applications_and_observations.topic: Maximum luminosity and the brightest sources
applications_and_observations.details: c^5/G bounds any luminosity; quasars and gamma-ray bursts are far below; black hole mergers approach it in gravitational waves; merging black holes briefly outshine the electromagnetic luminosity of the observable Universe (Exercise 9.45).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: c^5/G = 3.63e52 W; quasars and GRBs below 1e-10; merger peaks about 1e-3 (numerical simulations) to 0.01 (point-mass estimate).

applications_and_observations.details: Time delays within +/- d/c between sites give sky rings; three detectors give two patches; polarization from non-aligned detectors gives inclination; electromagnetic counterparts can pin down position.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: LIGO sites separated by about 3000 km (light time about 10 ms, our estimate).

applications_and_observations.details: Signals below the broadband noise are extracted by computer filtering; long waveforms like neutron star inspirals can be found below the burst threshold.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: A 200 Hz burst of 1e-22 is near the noise level of current LIGO ('a 1e-22 detector').

applications_and_observations.details: Three drag-free spacecraft with transponded 2-W lasers and time-delay interferometry; Pathfinder demonstrated free fall at the L1 point.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Arms 2.5e6 km; 1 AU heliocentric orbit trailing Earth by 20 degrees; 60-degree opening angle reduces response by sin 60 = 0.866; launch mid-2030s.

applications_and_observations.details: Einstein Telescope (Europe) and Cosmic Explorer (USA) would be about ten times more sensitive than Advanced LIGO, observing neutron star and stellar black hole mergers essentially throughout the Universe.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Operation probably after 2035 (as of mid-2021 writing).

applications_and_observations.topic: Standard-siren distances and the Hubble-Lemaitre constant
applications_and_observations.details: LIGO-Virgo assign distances to all binary detections with the siren method and correct masses for redshift; sirens can calibrate the cosmic expansion rate.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Forward-Berman era bars: binary neutron star range about 1 kpc; LIGO-Virgo by 2021: beyond 100 Mpc.

applications_and_observations.details: Because eccentricity decays faster than the separation, the system will be almost circular by the time it reaches the ground-based band, one or two minutes before merger.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: e below 1e-5 on entering the LIGO band (quoted from Andersson 2019).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Geometrized units G = c = 1 throughout: masses, times and lengths in metres; luminosity dimensionless with unit c^5/G = 3.63e52 W.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Solar mass about 1.477 km; the book uses 1.4 solar masses = 2.07 km.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Signature (-,+,+,+); indices raised and lowered with the Minkowski metric eta in linearized theory.
h-bar_{alpha beta} = h_{alpha beta} - (1/2) eta_{alpha beta} h; equal to h in TT gauge.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The reading copy's OCR renders the bar as a tilde in places.

notation_and_conventions.convention: h^TT_{jk} denotes transverse-traceless components; h_+ denotes h_xx^TT = -h_yy^TT for a wave along z; the cross amplitude is written h_xy^TT.
A comma denotes partial differentiation; subscript 0 is the time coordinate, so h_{xx,00} is the second time derivative.
Oscillating solutions are written with complex exponentials; the physical quantity is the real part, which must be taken before forming products such as energies.
Angle brackets denote averages over one period; double angle brackets in Exercise 9.50 denote averages over a period and a wavelength.
I^{lm} = integral of T^00 x^l x^m with no trace removal and no factor 3 (MTW convention); the trace-free version is printed as a barred I.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Other texts define Q_ij = integral rho (3 x_i x_j - r^2 delta_ij).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Omega denotes the source or wave angular frequency in general formulas; in binary sections omega is the orbital angular frequency and the wave frequency is 2 omega.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Eq. 9.144 writes (M Omega) where the orbital omega is meant.

notation_and_conventions.convention: m is each star's mass in §9.4; M is each star's mass in the Hulse-Taylor example of §9.5; in §9.6 M = m1 + m2 is the total mass, mu the reduced mass and script M the chirp mass.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Overloaded M is an easy trap across §§9.5-9.6.

notation_and_conventions.convention: iota is the angle between the orbital normal and the line of sight, face-on iota = 0; the x axis in the sky plane is chosen so that the orbit lies in the x-z plane when iota = pi/2.

notation_and_conventions.item: Riemann index order in geodesic deviation
notation_and_conventions.convention: d^2 xi^alpha/d tau^2 = R^alpha_{mu nu beta} U^mu U^nu xi^beta, equivalently -R^i_{0j0} xi^j for the tidal acceleration.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Sign follows the book's Chapter 6 convention.

notation_and_conventions.convention: xi is a gauge vector (9.14), a connecting vector (9.25) and a spring stretch (9.35); phi is a response phase, a polar angle and a Newtonian potential; R is a response amplitude, a source size and |x - y|; psi is a phase shift (9.119) and an orbital phase (9.159); A is a plane-wave amplitude tensor, a wave amplitude and a mass oscillation amplitude.

margin_notes.summary: Footnote 1: complex solutions are used for convenience and the real part is taken at the end, avoiding separate sine and cosine bookkeeping.

Footnote 2 (recovered from rendered page): wavelength and frequency of light depend on the observer, so asking whether the wave changes the laser wavelength is not frame-invariant and is best avoided in explaining interferometers.
Footnote 3 (missing from the reading copy, recovered from rendered page): explains the parsec (3.0857e16 m), typical star, galaxy and intergalactic scales, and its origin in parallax.
Footnote 4 (recovered from rendered page): a planar array's radiation in oblique directions cancels between neighbouring oscillators, which is why only the downstream direction was considered.
Footnote 5: the Chapel Hill proceedings reveal the conceptual confusions of the 1950s that later work resolved; see Blum et al. (2018).
Parenthetical warning that quadrupole-moment conventions vary between texts; the book follows Misner, Thorne and Wheeler.
Caution that the quadrupole approximation for self-gravitating sources is justified only by reference, and that the energy flux formula should be used only in linearized theory.
Figure 9.4 caption lists latitude-longitude coordinates of LIGO Hanford, Livingston, Virgo, GEO600, KAGRA and LIGO-India, inviting readers to view them in a mapping tool.
Bibliography notes that proving the quadrupole formula for strongly self-gravitating systems took decades (Damour, Futamase, Blanchet).

notable.summary: Step-by-step construction of the TT gauge: show the gauge change preserves transversality, use tracelessness and U-orthogonality to fix the gauge vector, show one of the four U-conditions is automatic, extend to arbitrary superpositions, and show a static field cannot be put in TT form.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the core algebra the text skips and reveals why TT gauge is a statement about radiation, not static fields.

notable.summary: Ask whether a small freely falling bowl of soup feels an acceleration and sloshes when a wave passes.
skills: distinguishing free fall from tidal effects
notable.why_notable: Short conceptual probe that separates coordinate rest, local inertial frames and tidal stretching.

notable.summary: Compare two metric perturbations that both satisfy the field and gauge equations, show their curvatures coincide, and find the gauge vector relating them.
notable.why_notable: Concrete demonstration that different-looking wave metrics can describe the same geometry, addressing the 'wavy coordinates' worry.

notable.summary: Use the plus-wave metric to find the coordinate speed of light, the round-trip proper time to particles on the x and y axes, and discuss whether the difference depends on gauge and what a chain of metre sticks would give.
skills: null curves in a perturbed metric
notable.why_notable: The distance-monitor principle of interferometers, with interpretive questions that expose common confusions.

notable.summary: Solve the sourced Helmholtz equation by separation of variables in spherical harmonics, identify Bessel and Hankel functions, and obtain general multipole amplitudes, recovering the monopole solution and assessing neglected terms.
notable.why_notable: Gives the rigorous backbone for the slow-motion argument and shows why higher multipoles are suppressed by powers of source size over wavelength.

notable.summary: Compare the vibrating spring with a system of two short-spring pairs whose stresses are not transmitted over the large separation, showing the omega term (proportional to l_0 A) disappears.
notable.why_notable: Shows physically that stresses, not just mass displacements, generate radiation, a subtle point behind the virial identity.

notable.summary: Derive the chirp time, time to merger, remaining orbital phase and the luminosity-phase relation from the frequency-evolution equation.
notable.why_notable: Builds the scaling toolkit used throughout gravitational-wave astronomy.

notable.summary: For an eccentric binary derive orbit-averaged energy and angular momentum loss, then the decay rates of semi-major axis, eccentricity and period, and verify the Hulse-Taylor prediction.
notable.why_notable: Connects the chapter's formalism to the precision test quoted in the text.

difficulty.notes: The propagation part (§9.2) is compact and elegant but assumes fluency with Chapter 8 gauge manipulations and leaves the key TT algebra to exercises. The detection section is long, largely qualitative and very accessible, apart from the radar-ranging calculation. Generation and energy (§§9.4-9.5) are the mathematical peak: Helmholtz integration with Gauss's theorem, tensor virial identity, TT projection, a planar sum with a convergence factor, and angular tensor integrals, with several printed sign and typo slips that can derail a careful reader. §9.6 is algebraically light and conceptually rich. Symbol overloading (xi, phi, R, M, psi) and frequent forward references add friction; the physical interpretation is excellent throughout.

Black holes, gravitational lensing and Mercury's precession; black hole mergers' luminosity.
Antenna patterns, detected signals, source populations and data analysis beyond this chapter.
Primordial waves and CMB polarization, cosmological luminosity distance, and siren measurements of the Hubble-Lemaitre constant.
Quadrupole convention, quantum limit, Isaacson stress-energy tensor, variational derivations of wave energy.
Plane-fronted waves with parallel rays.

teaching_gems.gem: Let the TT gauge 'prove' that nothing happens to free particles, then overturn the conclusion by computing the proper distance.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A deliberately provoked paradox makes the coordinate-versus-invariant distinction unforgettable and answers Einstein's 'wavy coordinates' worry.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Split view: TT coordinate grid where particles sit still versus a proper-distance view where they oscillate, linked by one time slider.

teaching_gems.gem: Rewrite the wave's action as a Newtonian-looking tidal force in a local inertial frame so that other forces can simply be added.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns curvature into something learners can put into F = ma, and resolves the rigid-ruler question with force comparison.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Mass-spring chain under a wave with an adjustable internal stiffness; readouts of tidal versus elastic force.

teaching_gems.gem: Differentiate the radar return time so the integral collapses to wave values at emission and reception.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A small calculus trick yields a surprising, testable result and naturally leads to interferometers as two-arm clocks.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Space-time diagram of a photon bouncing between free masses in a wave, with the return-time derivative plotted live and the reflection-time term appearing as the wave direction tilts.

teaching_gems.gem: Build the interferometer by placing arms inside the ring-of-particles picture.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Links an abstract polarization diagram to real detector geometry, explaining sensitivity and blind spots in one image.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Drag arms over the Figure 9.1 ring and see the differential arm signal for each polarization and direction.

teaching_gems.gem: Reuse one spring-and-masses toy as detector, emitter and energy calibrator.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Continuity reduces cognitive load and demonstrates that absorption and emission are two faces of the same coupling.
teaching_gems.app_idea: A single oscillator widget with three modes (receive, transmit, absorb-and-reradiate) that share parameters.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive the wave energy flux by making the detector absorb energy and then showing its parameters cancel.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Delivers a field-theory result with only energy conservation and interference, and shows why the answer is a property of the wave.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Energy-ledger simulation where changing oscillator mass, damping or density never changes the computed dF/dA.

teaching_gems.gem: Explain detectability by comparing forces, not amplitudes: waves fall as 1/r, tides as 1/r^3.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Resolves the puzzle of detecting waves from sources whose static gravity is unmeasurable, with a one-line scaling.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Log-log plot of wave tidal acceleration and Newtonian tidal acceleration versus distance with a draggable crossover.

teaching_gems.gem: Use scale-freedom to show luminosity depends only on orbits remaining, and that the chirp reveals the chirp mass.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Dimensional reasoning produces striking, mass-independent predictions and sets up standard sirens with minimal algebra.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Chirp explorer: choose masses, watch waveform, luminosity and remaining-orbit counter; rescale masses to see curves collapse when plotted against orbits left.

teaching_gems.gem: Frame gravitational-wave astronomy as listening rather than looking.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives novices a coherent mental model for phase-coherent detection, poor directionality, networks and chirps.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Audio sonification of inspirals with adjustable chirp mass alongside a microphone-array localization mini-game.

teaching_gems.gem: Bound any luminosity by c^5/G with a black-hole-formation argument.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A short, units-based argument that applies to all radiation and puts merger luminosities in perspective.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Luminosity ladder from the Sun to quasars to merging black holes on a log scale capped by c^5/G.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed Christoffel symbol for the exact plane wave reads Gamma^v_xx = 2 f-dot/f (and 2 g-dot/g); for the metric -du dv + f^2 dx^2 + g^2 dy^2 it should be 2 f f-dot (and 2 g g-dot). The linearized solution is also printed as f approximately 1 - epsilon(a) instead of epsilon(u).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners checking the calculation get inconsistent Riemann components and suspect their own algebra.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the Christoffel computation explicitly with g^{uv} = -2 and flag the correction.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. 9.58 as printed has h_+(z - t) multiplying dx^2 but h_+(t - z) multiplying dy^2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The two arguments differ by sign, which for a general waveform would not be the same wave.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use a single retarded-time argument h_+(t - z) in both terms.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. 9.83 is printed with exponent -i Omega (r - t), opposite to Eq. 9.74's outgoing form, and Eq. 9.106 carries a minus sign that is inconsistent with Eqs. 9.83 and 9.107 once d^2 I/dt^2 = -Omega^2 D e^{-i Omega t} is used; the second line of Eq. 9.107 is labelled h_xx with a stray bracket where h_xy = (2/r) d^2 I_xy/dt^2 is meant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sign and label slips in the central generation formula undermine confidence and propagate into polarization signs.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present h-bar_jk = (2/r) d^2 I_jk(t - r)/dt^2 and derive the TT components from it, noting the printed variants.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. 9.88's middle line drops the factor m, and Eq. 9.92 prints A where A^2 is needed (Eq. 9.93 has A^2).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Carry m and A^2 explicitly; use a dimension check as a teaching moment.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. 9.124 is printed with 8 I^{xy} where 8 (I_xy)^2 is required.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The flux formula looks non-quadratic, blocking the reader from verifying Eq. 9.126.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write both polarizations' squares explicitly before simplifying.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. 9.147 converts dP/dt = -2.40263e-12 to -7.2e-15 s/yr; the correct conversion is about -7.6e-5 s/yr (multiply by 3.156e7 s). Also the text after Eq. 9.133 cites 'Eq. 9.70' for the amplitude estimate, which is Eq. 9.101.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A reader comparing with the earlier -6e-6 s/yr estimate and the stated factor 12 finds a nine-order-of-magnitude contradiction.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Recompute the conversion with the learner and check it against 12 times the circular estimate.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Hulse-Taylor distance is printed as 8 kpc = 2.4e17 m; 8 kpc is about 2.5e20 m (footnote 3's own parsec value gives this). The quoted amplitude 1e-20 matches the mis-printed distance; with the correct distance 2 m l_0^2 omega^2/r gives about 4e-23 (our estimate). The laboratory-generator amplitude 1e-34/r is also about three orders of magnitude larger than the stated parameters give (2 m omega^2 l_0 A about 1.5e-37, so about 2e-37/r).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Order-of-magnitude intuition built on these numbers will be off by large factors.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Have learners redo both estimates in geometrized units as an exercise in unit conversion.

tutor_notes: Open with a question: 'If a gravitational wave passes, do two free-floating marbles move apart? How would you know?' Let the learner discover that coordinates cannot answer it and a measurement of distance or light travel time can.

Recommended order: wave equation and null k, gauge counting to two polarizations, TT coordinates paradox, proper distance, geodesic deviation as tidal force, ring picture, then detectors. Keep generation and energy for after the learner is comfortable with h as a strain.
Check understanding of TT gauge by asking why particles stay at fixed coordinates yet move apart, and why this is not a contradiction.

For polarization, ask the learner to predict the pattern after rotating the ring by 45 degrees, and contrast with light's 90 degrees; ask which polarization an L-shaped detector with arms on x and y misses for overhead waves.
When the ruler question comes up, compare magnitudes: tidal acceleration h L omega^2 with interatomic forces; emphasize that detectors avoid rulers by timing light between free masses.
For interferometers, stress 'two clocks compared' rather than 'wavelength ruler'; if asked whether the laser light is stretched, point to footnote 2 and the return-time derivation.

Common learner question: 'Why is gravitational radiation quadrupolar?' Answer with conservation: constant total mass-energy kills monopole, fixed centre of mass kills dipole, and connect to electromagnetism's charge conservation.
Quick estimation drills: h ~ (M/r) v^2 for a binary; strain times 4 km for mirror displacement; L ~ (32/5)(M omega)^{10/3} in units of c^5/G. Always convert masses to metres first.
For the energy flux, narrate Feynman's sticky beads before any mathematics, then highlight that the detector parameters cancel; warn that the formula is an average valid in linearized theory.
When discussing binaries, clarify omega (orbital) versus 2 omega (wave), and total versus individual mass; ask the learner to derive chirp mass for two 1.4 solar mass stars (about 1.22 solar masses).
Standard sirens: ask 'What would you need to know to turn loudness into distance?' Guide to chirp mass from frequency drift, then inclination from polarization, then redshift degeneracy.
Flag the printed slips (Eqs. 9.83, 9.92, 9.106-9.107, 9.124, 9.147, the 8 kpc conversion) proactively if the learner is working from the book, so they do not lose time doubting correct algebra.

Learners at lower levels can skip the Helmholtz-Gauss derivation and accept h-bar_jk = (2/r) d^2 I_jk/dt^2 with the analogy to dipole radiation; advanced learners should do Exercise 9.29 or the projector derivation.
Update dated statements when relevant: pulsar timing evidence for a nanohertz background (2023), LISA adoption (2024), and the growing catalogue of LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA events.
